title: SQL, modelling and ORMs
blurb: Joins, indexes, transactions, N+1, migrations. The biggest gap in most self-taught developers' knowledge, and the one interviewers probe hardest for CRUD roles.

questions.q: What is the difference between an INNER JOIN and a LEFT JOIN?
choices: LEFT is faster, because it can stop reading the right table after one match
INNER keeps only matched rows; LEFT keeps every left row, with NULLs for no match
INNER can return duplicate rows, while LEFT always returns each left row just once
LEFT joins on the primary key only, while INNER can join on any column at all
questions.why: "Users and their orders" with INNER silently drops users who never ordered. For "all users with their order count" you need LEFT, and `COUNT(o.id)` rather than `COUNT(*)` so those users score 0. A LEFT JOIN repeats a left row once per match, so it can duplicate too.
questions.asked: You will be asked to write a JOIN; this is the distinction that gets tested.

questions.q: Why does this return no rows for users without a paid order?
questions.code:
SELECT u.name, o.total
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid';
choices: A LEFT JOIN cannot be filtered with WHERE; the filter belongs in HAVING
status has no index, so the planner drops the unmatched rows early
The WHERE rejects the NULL rows, so the LEFT JOIN acts like an INNER JOIN
The ON condition is written backwards and should compare u.id to o.user_id instead
questions.why: For an unmatched user, `o.status` is NULL and `NULL = 'paid'` is not true, so WHERE removes exactly the rows the LEFT JOIN kept. Move the condition into the ON clause to keep them. Equality is symmetric, and indexes never change results.
questions.asked: A genuinely tricky one that comes up in real reporting bugs.

questions.q: What does an index actually do?
choices: Caches recent query results and invalidates them when the table changes
Keeps a compressed copy of the table that the planner reads instead
Enforces uniqueness on a column, which is why every table needs one
Keeps a sorted structure over some columns: faster reads, slower writes
questions.why: Every index must be updated on every insert, update and delete, and takes storage. Index what you filter, join and sort on, not every column; an index on a low-cardinality boolean usually earns nothing. Only a unique index enforces uniqueness.
questions.asked: Then: "so why not index everything?" The write cost is the answer.

questions.q: Why might an index on `email` not be used here?
questions.code: SELECT * FROM users WHERE LOWER(email) = 'a@b.com';
choices: Indexes are never used for text columns, only for numbers and dates
SELECT * forces a full table scan, whatever indexes the table has
Wrapping the column in a function makes the predicate non-sargable
Equality on strings must be written with LIKE to consider an index
questions.why: The index stores raw values, not lowercased ones. Fixes: store the email normalised, use a case-insensitive collation (the SQL Server default; `citext` in Postgres), or index the expression: `CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email))` in Postgres, a functional key in MySQL 8.0.13+, an indexed computed column in SQL Server.
questions.asked: Checks you can read a WHERE clause the way the planner does.

questions.q: What is wrong with this code as the list grows?
choices: The awaits run the customer queries in parallel and exhaust the pool
LIMIT without ORDER BY attaches customers to the wrong orders
Each customer query holds a row lock until the whole loop completes
It runs one query for the list plus one per row: the N+1 problem
questions.why: 100 orders means 101 round trips, and the page gets slower with every row. Fetch the customers in one query (a join, or `WHERE id = ANY($1)` in Postgres / `IN (...)` elsewhere). ORMs hide the same loop: EF Core does not lazy-load by default, so there it usually comes from a query inside a loop exactly like this.
questions.asked: Near-guaranteed for any role using an ORM. Saying how you would detect it (log the SQL) is the strong part.

questions.q: What does a database transaction guarantee?
choices: Its statements run faster, because the engine skips the write-ahead log
It locks the whole table, so one user at a time can read or write it
It retries automatically after any failure until every one of its statements succeeds
All its statements commit together or none do, and commits survive a crash
questions.why: ACID: atomic (all or nothing), consistent (constraints hold), isolated (others do not see partial work), durable (a commit survives a crash, thanks to the log). The money transfer is the canonical example. Locking is usually per row, and retrying is your job.
questions.asked: The money-transfer example is expected; the follow-up is which statements belong inside the transaction.

questions.q: What is a lost update, and which fix prevents it without holding locks while the user edits?
choices: A rollback discards a saved change; commit each statement on its own
Two edits of one row overwrite each other; check a version in UPDATE ... WHERE
A row is deleted mid-edit; add ON DELETE CASCADE to its child tables
A stale cache hides the change; disable caching for that table entirely
questions.why: Both users read version 5; the first writes and bumps it to 6; the second's `UPDATE ... WHERE id = @id AND version = 5` matches zero rows, so you return 409 instead of silently overwriting. Pessimistic row locks also work but hold locks across user think-time.
questions.asked: Every collaborative CRUD app has this problem; optimistic concurrency is the answer interviewers want.

questions.q: What does NULL mean in SQL, and why is `= NULL` wrong?
choices: NULL is stored as an empty string, so compare with = '' instead
NULL equals zero in numeric columns, so compare with = 0 instead
NULL means unknown, so = NULL is never true; use IS NULL instead
= NULL works in every engine; IS NULL is just the ANSI spelling
questions.why: Any comparison with NULL is unknown, and WHERE keeps only true. This is why `NOT IN (subquery)` returns nothing when the subquery contains a NULL, and why COUNT(col) skips NULLs. SQL Server's legacy `ANSI_NULLS OFF` made `= NULL` work; it is deprecated.
questions.asked: Junior material, but the NOT IN follow-up catches experienced people too.

questions.q: What is normalisation, and when would you deliberately denormalise?
choices: Converting every column to text, so that the schema can change freely
Splitting one database across servers so each holds part of the rows
Renaming tables and columns to one convention across the schema
Each fact lives in one place; denormalise when reads justify the cost
questions.why: Third normal form is the sane default. Deliberate exceptions: a cached counter, a stored order total (the price at the time of sale must not follow the product's current price), a flattened search table. Splitting across servers is sharding.
questions.asked: The stored-order-total example is the answer that shows you have built a real system.

questions.q: How do you model a many-to-many relationship?
choices: A comma-separated list of ids stored in a text column on one side
A JSON array of related ids stored in a column on each table
A join table holding both foreign keys, with a composite primary key
A nullable foreign key on each table pointing at one row on the other
questions.why: Students and courses become an enrolments table. The join table is also the natural home for attributes of the relationship itself (enrolled_at, grade). Lists in a column cannot carry foreign keys or be indexed and joined cleanly.
questions.asked: A modelling basic; the attributes-on-the-relationship follow-up shows real experience.

questions.q: As a portable rule, what does `GROUP BY` require of the SELECT list?
choices: Each selected column must be covered by an index on the grouped table
Each selected column must be grouped or wrapped in an aggregate
Only grouped columns may appear; aggregates need a separate query
Nothing: the engine picks a value from any row in each group for you
questions.why: Otherwise the engine cannot know which row's value to show. Postgres, and MySQL with ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY (the default since 5.7.5), also accept columns functionally dependent on a grouped primary key. MySQL without that mode picks arbitrary values, which produced silently wrong reports; SQL Server applies the strict rule.
questions.asked: Checks you know the rule and why it exists, not just the error message.

questions.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
choices: They are interchangeable; HAVING is the older spelling kept for compatibility
HAVING filters joined rows; WHERE filters rows from the first table only
WHERE cannot appear in a query with GROUP BY, so HAVING replaces it
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregating
questions.why: `WHERE status = 'paid'` narrows the input rows; `HAVING COUNT(*) > 5` narrows the resulting groups. Filtering in WHERE when you can is also faster, because fewer rows reach the aggregation.
questions.asked: A quick check before a live SQL exercise.

questions.q: What is SQL injection, and what actually prevents it?
choices: Input becoming part of the SQL text; prevented by capping input length
Input becoming part of the SQL text; prevented by parameterised queries
Input becoming part of the SQL text; prevented by stripping quote marks
Input becoming part of the SQL text; prevented by any ORM in all cases
questions.why: Parameters are sent separately from the query text, so input can never become code. Stripping quotes fails on numeric contexts and encodings. ORMs parameterise by default, but raw SQL escape hatches and dynamic ORDER BY are still yours to get right.
questions.asked: Universal. The wrong answer is "sanitise the input".

questions.q: What does `EXPLAIN` (Postgres, MySQL) show you about a query?
choices: How long the query took, broken down per table it touched
Which sessions ran the query most often in the last hour
The planner's strategy: scans, join order and estimated rows
Whether the syntax is valid, without consulting any statistics
questions.why: A sequential scan of a large table where you expected an index is the classic finding. Plain EXPLAIN does not run the query; Postgres `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` does, giving real timings and row counts so you can see where the estimate was wrong. In SQL Server the equivalent is the estimated or actual execution plan.
questions.asked: "How would you diagnose a slow query?" This is the first move.

questions.q: What is a database migration, and why are migrations versioned?
choices: Copying data between servers when a database moves to new hardware
Switching database vendor, for example from MySQL to Postgres
Ordered, checked-in schema changes, so every environment converges
A scheduled backup and restore that resets staging to production
questions.why: Schema changes are code and belong in the repository and the pipeline, applied in order and recorded so each runs once. The hard part is the rollout on a live table, which is the next question.
questions.asked: Checks you treat the schema as code rather than something edited by hand in production.

questions.q: You must add a required column, whose value is computed from existing data, to a large live table. What is the safe sequence?
choices: Add it NOT NULL with a DEFAULT in one statement, then run one big UPDATE
Add it nullable, backfill in batches, write it from new code, then NOT NULL
Drop and recreate the table with the column, then reload it from backup
Add it NOT NULL inside a transaction, so the app simply waits until the backfill ends
questions.why: Expand/contract: batches keep locks short and old and new code can run side by side during a rolling deploy. A constant default alone is metadata-only in Postgres 11+ and SQL Server Enterprise, but a computed value still needs a backfill, and one giant UPDATE locks rows and bloats the log.
questions.asked: A strong mid-level question: it tests deployment thinking, not just SQL.

questions.q: What does a foreign key constraint buy you?
choices: Faster joins, because the planner uses the key as a ready-made index
Indexes created on both columns automatically in every database engine
The database refuses rows pointing at a missing parent, and guards deletes
Nothing that an application check cannot do equally well just before inserting
questions.why: Application checks race and are bypassed by scripts and admin tools. The FK column is not indexed automatically in Postgres or SQL Server (MySQL InnoDB does create one), and an unindexed FK makes parent deletes scan the child table.
questions.asked: Checks you trust the database for integrity, and know the indexing gotcha.

questions.q: When would you use a composite index, and does column order matter?
choices: Column order never matters, since the planner reorders the columns itself
For filters on several columns; it serves a leading prefix, not a later column
Only for unique constraints; ordinary filters should use single indexes
Never: several single-column indexes always beat one composite index
questions.why: An index on (tenant_id, created_at) serves `WHERE tenant_id = ?` and `WHERE tenant_id = ? ORDER BY created_at`, but not `WHERE created_at > ?` on its own. Put equality columns first. Skip scans (MySQL 8.0.13+, Postgres 18) can sometimes use a later column, but do not design around them.
questions.asked: Checks you can design an index for a real query rather than index columns one by one.

questions.q: What is the difference between `DELETE`, `TRUNCATE` and `DROP`?
choices: DELETE removes chosen rows one by one; TRUNCATE empties it fast; DROP removes it
DELETE removes the table; TRUNCATE removes chosen rows; DROP empties it fast
They are one command with three spellings, kept for portability between SQL engines
DELETE cannot be rolled back, but TRUNCATE and DROP can both be undone at will
questions.why: TRUNCATE takes no WHERE, resets identity values in SQL Server and MySQL (Postgres only with RESTART IDENTITY) and fires no per-row DELETE triggers. It is transactional in Postgres and SQL Server but commits implicitly in MySQL, so "can I roll it back?" depends on the engine. Knowing which one someone ran is the first question when data goes missing.
questions.asked: A classic; the engine-dependent rollback detail is the senior touch.

questions.q: How should you store money?
choices: A float, rounding to two decimal places only when displaying it
A string, so the exact digits the user typed are always preserved
A double, since its extra precision removes the rounding errors
Integer minor units or a fixed-precision DECIMAL, never a binary float
questions.why: Binary floats cannot represent 0.10 exactly, so sums drift; a double only moves the error further out. DECIMAL(19,4) or integer cents are exact and still support arithmetic. Store the currency alongside: a number without a currency is not money.
questions.asked: A quick filter; the currency-column follow-up shows real e-commerce experience.

questions.q: How should you store timestamps?
choices: As local time strings, so they read correctly for each user on screen
As Unix integers in the server's local time, so date arithmetic stays simple
In the server's own time zone, since that is where the rows are written
In UTC, in a zone-aware type such as timestamptz, converting for display
questions.why: Local times are ambiguous twice a year and meaningless across regions. Postgres `timestamptz` stores UTC; SQL Server has `datetimeoffset` (or `datetime2` holding UTC by convention); MySQL `TIMESTAMP` converts to UTC while `DATETIME` does not. Keep the user's IANA zone separately if you need their wall-clock time.
questions.asked: Every app with users in more than one place hits this; the "one day off" bug is the follow-up.

questions.q: What is a database connection pool, and why does it matter?
choices: A cache of recent query results, shared between the app's instances
A set of read replicas that the driver load-balances SELECT queries across
A reused, capped set of open connections, so the server is not swamped
A queue of pending transactions the database commits in batches
questions.why: Opening a connection costs round trips and server memory. Pool exhaustion is a classic outage: a slow query holds connections, requests queue for one, and the app appears to hang while the database looks healthy.
questions.asked: Checks you can explain "the app hangs but the database is fine".

questions.q: What does `SELECT *` cost you in application code?
choices: Nothing: the engine expands it to the same column list at no cost
A full table scan on every query, whatever indexes the table has
It disables the plan cache, so the query recompiles on each run
Extra data on the wire, breakage when columns change, no index-only scans
questions.why: Naming columns makes the contract explicit and stops a new BLOB column from silently doubling every response. A covering index can only answer the query alone if the query asks for the columns it holds. `SELECT *` does not by itself cause a table scan.
questions.asked: A code-review staple; the index-only scan point is the deeper answer.

questions.q: In SQL Server (or MySQL InnoDB), what is the difference between a clustered and a non-clustered index?
choices: A clustered index is held entirely in memory; a non-clustered one lives on disk
Non-clustered indexes cannot be unique; only the clustered one can be
The clustered index is the table, stored in key order; others point to it
A clustered index is read-only and rebuilt nightly from the others
questions.why: There is one clustered index per table because the rows can only be stored in one order. A random GUID key makes inserts land all over it and fragment it, which is why sequential GUIDs exist. Postgres stores tables as heaps; its CLUSTER command is a one-off reorder.
questions.asked: A standard SQL Server question; the GUID key follow-up is common in .NET interviews.

questions.q: When is a document store a better fit than a relational database?
choices: Whenever the app must scale, since relational databases cannot shard
Whenever the data grows beyond a few gigabytes on a single server
Self-contained documents, varied schema, few joins or multi-row transactions
Whenever the team would rather not write SQL or manage migrations
questions.why: Most CRUD apps are relational: orders reference customers who have addresses. Choosing a document store to avoid schema work usually means writing the joins, and the integrity checks, in application code instead. Relational databases handle far more than a few gigabytes.
questions.asked: An opinion question. "It depends on the access pattern" is the beginning of a good answer.

questions.q: What does a UNIQUE constraint do that an application check does not?
choices: It validates faster than a SELECT, since the check skips the table
It gives users a clearer error message than application code can
It holds under concurrency: two simultaneous inserts cannot both pass
It can enforce uniqueness across several different tables in a single rule
questions.why: Check-then-insert is a race: both requests read "no such email" and both insert. The constraint is the only atomic check, so catch the violation and turn it into a 409. Keep the application check too, for a friendly message.
questions.asked: A quietly excellent question about whether you think in terms of concurrency.

questions.q: What is the repository pattern, and is it worth adding on top of EF Core?
choices: A pattern EF Core requires before a DbContext can be registered in DI
A NoSQL-only pattern for mapping stored documents onto objects in memory
A data-access seam: useful for domain queries, arguable if it only forwards calls
Always worth it, because it lets you swap databases without changing code
questions.why: A DbContext is already a unit of work over repository-like DbSets. A thin repository that forwards every call adds indirection; one that names domain queries ("GetOverdueInvoices") adds value. Swapping databases behind it is rarer and harder than the slogan suggests.
questions.asked: A .NET favourite. Interviewers want a considered opinion, not a doctrine.

questions.q: You need the 10 most recent orders per customer. What is the idiomatic SQL?
choices: GROUP BY customer_id with ORDER BY created_at DESC and a LIMIT 10
SELECT DISTINCT customer_id ordered by created_at DESC, then LIMIT 10
A subquery per customer, run from application code in a loop over ids
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC) <= 10
questions.why: Number rows within each customer and keep those numbered 10 or less, filtering in an outer query or CTE because window results cannot appear in WHERE. GROUP BY collapses each customer to one row, and LIMIT applies to the whole result. Postgres LATERAL and SQL Server CROSS APPLY are alternatives.
questions.asked: The classic "top N per group" task in live SQL rounds.

questions.q: In EF Core, which parts of this query run in SQL?
questions.code:
var names = db.Orders
    .Where(o => o.Status == "paid")
    .AsEnumerable()
    .Where(o => o.Total > 100)
    .Select(o => o.CustomerName)
    .ToList();
choices: All of it: EF Core translates the whole chain once ToList() finally runs
Only the Status filter; the Total filter and Select run in memory
None of it: AsEnumerable() loads the whole Orders table first
The two Where filters; only the Select projection runs in memory
questions.why: `AsEnumerable()` switches from IQueryable to LINQ to Objects: everything before it becomes SQL, everything after runs on the materialised rows. Here every column of every paid order is fetched, then filtered in C#. Keep it only for a step that cannot be translated, as late as possible.
questions.asked: Checks you can see where the database boundary is in a LINQ chain.

questions.q: How do you paginate a feed reliably while new rows keep arriving?
choices: OFFSET with a larger page size, so there are fewer page boundaries
Cache page 1 and compute OFFSET for later pages relative to that copy
Sort by id ascending and use OFFSET, since ids never change once set
Keyset: filter past the last row's (created_at, id) and order by both
questions.why: Keyset pagination is stable under inserts and stays fast at any depth, because the index seeks to the cursor. Postgres and MySQL accept `WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2)`; SQL Server needs `created_at < @c OR (created_at = @c AND id < @id)`. The id tiebreaker makes the order total.
questions.asked: Pairs API design with database knowledge; the tiebreaker is what interviewers listen for.

questions.q: Why do most tables use a surrogate key (an id) rather than a natural key such as email?
choices: Databases cannot index text columns, so keys have to be numeric ids
Natural values can change or repeat, and a key must stay stable
Natural keys are slower to insert, as they must be generated first
Surrogate keys are required before a table can have foreign keys
questions.why: People change email addresses, and every foreign key pointing at the old one would have to change too. Keep a UNIQUE constraint on the natural value. Natural keys are fine for truly stable codes such as ISO country codes.
questions.asked: A modelling basic that shows whether you have lived through a key change.

questions.q: What changes if you write `UNION ALL` instead of `UNION` here?
choices: Duplicates are kept, and the de-duplication step is skipped
Rows from both tables interleave instead of one set after the other
Columns are matched by name instead of by position in each SELECT
NULL emails are kept, which UNION would silently drop from the result
questions.why: `UNION` removes duplicate rows across the whole result, which costs a sort or hash; `UNION ALL` just appends. Use UNION ALL unless you need de-duplication. Both match columns by position, and neither guarantees order without ORDER BY.
questions.asked: A cheap performance win that also tests whether you know what UNION actually does.

questions.q: A query without ORDER BY returned rows in id order for months, then stopped. Why?
choices: The clustered index was dropped, and it is the only thing that sorts rows
Row order follows insertion time, so a bulk import reshuffled the table
Without ORDER BY the engine may return rows in whatever order is cheapest
A recent upgrade changed the database's default sort setting for tables
questions.why: Tables are unordered sets; without ORDER BY the order is whatever the plan produced. New statistics, a parallel scan or a different index change the plan and the order. Always ORDER BY, with a unique tiebreaker, when order matters.
questions.asked: Checks you do not depend on accidental behaviour, a common source of flaky tests and reports.

questions.q: The table has 5 rows; 2 have a NULL phone, and city is Leeds, Leeds, York, NULL, York. What does this return?
questions.code:
SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(phone), COUNT(DISTINCT city)
FROM customers;
questions.why: `COUNT(*)` counts rows; `COUNT(col)` counts non-NULL values; `COUNT(DISTINCT col)` counts distinct non-NULL values, so NULL is not a third city. This is why a LEFT JOIN report must count a column from the right-hand table.
questions.asked: A quick check of NULL handling in aggregates before a live SQL task.

questions.q: What is the main schema cost of soft delete (a deleted_at column) over deleting rows?
choices: Rows cannot be restored later, since deleted_at makes them read-only
Every query and unique rule must exclude deleted rows, or they leak back
Foreign keys stop working, because the parent row has left the table
The table is rebuilt on each delete, since deleted_at changes the row size
questions.why: Every read needs `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`, and a UNIQUE on email blocks re-registration unless it becomes a partial (Postgres) or filtered (SQL Server) unique index. Tables grow forever, and privacy erasure still needs real deletes. An archive table is the alternative.
questions.asked: A design trade-off question; the unique-constraint problem is the detail most candidates miss.

questions.q: What is the risk of declaring `ON DELETE CASCADE` on every foreign key?
choices: The engine ignores cascades inside explicit transactions, leaving orphans
Cascades are built on triggers, which slow every insert on child tables
Parents can no longer be deleted while any of their children still exist
One delete can silently remove large trees of rows across many tables
questions.why: Cascade suits owned children (an order and its lines); on references such as customer to invoices, one mistaken delete wipes financial history. Blocking deletes while children exist is what RESTRICT and NO ACTION do. SQL Server also rejects multiple cascade paths to one table.
questions.asked: Checks you choose delete behaviour per relationship rather than by habit.

questions.q: Why can a B-tree index on `name` not help with `WHERE name LIKE '%smith'`?
choices: LIKE is always evaluated after a full scan, whatever the pattern is
The index is sorted by leading characters, and the pattern fixes none
Indexes store only the first 10 characters of each text value they hold
B-tree indexes support only = comparisons, never LIKE or range filters
questions.why: `LIKE 'smith%'` becomes a range seek on the sorted index; a leading wildcard gives the seek nowhere to start. In Postgres the prefix case also needs the C collation or `text_pattern_ops`. For contains-search, use a trigram index (Postgres pg_trgm) or full-text search.
questions.asked: Search boxes are in every CRUD app; checks you know why the naive one gets slow.

questions.q: `created_at` is a timestamp column. This is meant to fetch all of March. What does it miss?
questions.code:
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2026-03-01' AND '2026-03-31';
choices: Orders on 1 March, since BETWEEN excludes both of its end points
Nothing: BETWEEN on timestamps widens each bound to the whole day
Orders from 31 March after midnight, as the end bound is 00:00:00
Orders in other zones, since string literals are always read as UTC
questions.why: BETWEEN is inclusive, and `'2026-03-31'` means midnight at the start of the 31st, so almost the whole last day is lost. Use a half-open range: `created_at >= '2026-03-01' AND created_at < '2026-04-01'`. That holds in Postgres, SQL Server and MySQL and stays index-friendly.
questions.asked: Every report has a date filter; this bug ships in most first attempts.

questions.q: When is a JSON column (Postgres jsonb, or JSON text in SQL Server) a reasonable choice?
choices: For any field that might change, so migrations are never needed again
For related ids, since a JSON array joins faster than a separate table
For loosely structured data stored and returned whole, rarely filtered
For money and dates, since JSON keeps their types more exactly than SQL
questions.why: Webhook payloads, per-tenant settings and third-party metadata fit well. Inside JSON you lose types, NOT NULL, foreign keys and easy indexing (Postgres needs GIN or expression indexes; SQL Server indexes computed columns). Once you filter or join on a field, promote it to a real column.
questions.asked: A judgement question: the strong answer names the signal for promoting a field to a column.

questions.q: Why add `created_at` and `updated_at` columns to most tables?
choices: The database needs them to order rows, since tables have no order
They replace backups, since old values can be rebuilt from them
They stop lost updates, since writes with an older stamp are rejected
They record when a row appeared or changed, for debugging and sync
questions.why: They answer "when did this change?" in support tickets and let clients sync with "changed since". They record when, not who or what: use an audit or history table for that. `updated_at` prevents lost updates only if you check it in the UPDATE's WHERE.
questions.asked: A cheap habit that interviewers read as operational experience.

questions.q: Two customers buy the last unit at the same moment. Which approach guarantees stock never goes negative in Postgres, SQL Server and MySQL alike?
choices: SELECT the quantity, check it is above zero in application code, then UPDATE it to quantity minus one
Wrap that SELECT and UPDATE in a transaction, since a transaction serialises concurrent writers
Run `UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE id = ? AND qty > 0` and treat zero affected rows as sold out
Set the transaction to REPEATABLE READ, so the second transaction's SELECT waits for the first to commit
questions.why: The conditional UPDATE is one atomic statement: the row is locked while the predicate is checked and the value written, so the second statement sees qty = 0 and matches nothing. Check-then-write has a gap between the read and the write, and a transaction at the default READ COMMITTED level does not close it: both transactions read 1. REPEATABLE READ changes what a transaction reads, not whether it waits, and what happens on the conflicting write then differs by engine, so it is not a portable fix. A CHECK (qty >= 0) constraint is a good backstop.
questions.asked: The classic stock or seat-booking race; the strong answer knows the check has to happen inside the write.

questions.q: Order 1 (total 100) has three lines and order 2 (total 50) has one, both for customer 1. What does this return, and why?
questions.code:
SELECT o.customer_id, SUM(o.total) AS spent
FROM orders o
JOIN order_lines l ON l.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY o.customer_id;
choices: 150, because SUM counts each order's total once however many lines it has
350, because the join repeats order 1 once per line before the SUM runs
An error, because o.total is neither grouped nor wrapped in an aggregate
400, because every order total is multiplied by the number of all lines
questions.why: The join produces one row per line, so order 1's total appears three times: 300 + 50. This join fan-out silently inflates sums; aggregate the lines in a subquery first, or sum from `orders` alone. SUM has no idea which rows are 'the same order'.
questions.asked: Inflated totals from a join are one of the most common reporting bugs, and interviewers like candidates who spot the fan-out before running it.

questions.q: `b.y` holds 2 and NULL; `a.x` holds 1, 2 and 3. What does this return in Postgres, SQL Server or SQLite?
questions.code:
SELECT x FROM a
WHERE x NOT IN (SELECT y FROM b);
choices: 1 and 3, the values of x that do not appear anywhere in b
1, 2 and 3, because a NULL in the list makes the subquery be ignored entirely
No rows, because x <> NULL is unknown, so no row passes the test
An error, because a subquery used with IN may not contain NULLs
questions.why: `x NOT IN (2, NULL)` expands to `x <> 2 AND x <> NULL`; the second part is unknown, so the whole test is never true. `NOT EXISTS` with a correlated subquery returns 1 and 3 as intended, which is why it is the safer anti-join.
questions.asked: The NOT IN trap separates people who know three-valued logic from people who have only read about it.

questions.q: You need every customer who has never placed an order. Which query is correct and portable?
choices: SELECT c.* FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL
SELECT c.* FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL
SELECT c.* FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.id IS NULL
SELECT c.* FROM customers c RIGHT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE c.id IS NULL
questions.why: A LEFT JOIN keeps every customer, and customers with no match get NULL for every order column, so filtering `o.id IS NULL` in WHERE keeps exactly those. Putting the test in ON just changes which orders match and still returns every customer; an INNER JOIN has already dropped them.
questions.asked: 'Find the rows with no match' is a standard whiteboard task; the strong answer also offers NOT EXISTS.

questions.q: What does `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sizes CROSS JOIN colours` return when sizes has 3 rows and colours has 4?
choices: 7, one row for every size followed by one row for every colour
4, one row for each colour paired with its first matching size
12, every size paired with every colour: the Cartesian product
3, because a cross join keeps only the rows of the left table
questions.why: A CROSS JOIN pairs every left row with every right row, so the count multiplies. It is useful for generating combinations such as product variants or a calendar grid; appending rows is UNION ALL, which gives 7.
questions.asked: Asked to check you know joins multiply rows, which explains accidental Cartesian products from a missing ON.

questions.q: `employees` has `id`, `name` and `manager_id` (another employee's id). How do you list each employee beside their manager's name, keeping the CEO who has no manager?
choices: SELECT e.name, m.name FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.id
SELECT e.name, m.name FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id
SELECT e.name, m.name FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.manager_id = e.id
SELECT name, manager_id FROM employees GROUP BY manager_id
questions.why: A self-join aliases the same table twice; the manager row is the one whose id equals this employee's manager_id. LEFT keeps the CEO with a NULL manager name. Joining `m.manager_id = e.id` goes the other way and lists each person's direct reports instead.
questions.asked: Self-joins come up with hierarchies and 'compare a row with another row of the same table'; aliasing clearly is the skill.

questions.q: For an INNER JOIN, what changes if you move `o.status = 'paid'` from the WHERE clause into the ON clause?
choices: Nothing in the result: for an inner join both places filter the same rows
Customers without a paid order are kept, with NULLs in the order columns
The filter now runs after grouping, so aggregate totals are different
The query fails, as ON may only compare columns from two different tables
questions.why: With an inner join, a row must satisfy both the join condition and the filter wherever you write them, and the planner treats them the same. The placement only matters for outer joins, where a condition in ON decides what matches while one in WHERE removes the NULL-extended rows.
questions.asked: A follow-up to the LEFT JOIN WHERE trap; knowing why it is harmless for INNER shows you understand the rule rather than memorising it.

questions.q: What does a FULL OUTER JOIN between `ledger` and `bank_statement` on transaction reference give you that a LEFT JOIN does not?
choices: Only the references present in both, with the columns of both sides
Every ledger row, plus a copy of each bank row for every ledger row
The ledger rows with no match, and nothing else from either of the two tables
Matched rows, plus unmatched rows from both sides with NULLs opposite
questions.why: FULL OUTER keeps unmatched rows from both tables, so a reconciliation can show entries missing from the bank and entries missing from the ledger in one pass. MySQL has no FULL OUTER JOIN; you emulate it with a LEFT JOIN UNION a RIGHT JOIN anti-join.
questions.asked: Reconciliation reports are a real use of FULL OUTER JOIN; mentioning the MySQL gap is a bonus.

questions.q: In Postgres, SQL Server or SQLite, `v` holds 10, NULL and 20. What do `AVG(v)`, `COUNT(v)` and `COUNT(*)` return?
choices: 10, 3, 3, because NULL is treated as zero by every aggregate
NULL, 2, 3, because any NULL input makes AVG return NULL
15, 3, 3, because COUNT always counts every row, whatever column it names
15, 2, 3, because aggregates skip NULLs but COUNT(*) counts rows
questions.why: SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX and COUNT(column) ignore NULLs, so the average is (10 + 20) / 2. COUNT(*) counts rows regardless. If a missing value should count as zero, say so with `AVG(COALESCE(v, 0))`, which gives 10.
questions.asked: A quick check that you know aggregates skip NULL, which changes averages in real reports.

questions.q: A dashboard shows revenue with `SELECT SUM(total) FROM orders WHERE created_at >= $1`. On a day with no orders, what does the API receive?
choices: 0, because SUM over no rows starts from zero
NULL, because SUM over zero rows returns NULL
No row at all, because nothing matched the filter
An error, because SUM needs at least one input row
questions.why: An aggregate without GROUP BY always returns exactly one row, and SUM of an empty set is NULL, not zero. Wrap it as `COALESCE(SUM(total), 0)` so the client does not print 'null' or crash on arithmetic. COUNT is the exception and returns 0.
questions.asked: The empty-period NULL shows up as a real production bug in dashboards; COALESCE is the expected fix.

questions.q: What does `GROUP BY region` do with rows whose region is NULL?
choices: It drops them, because NULL cannot be compared with any group key
It puts each NULL row in its own group, as no two NULLs are equal
It puts all of them together in a single group with a NULL key
It raises an error unless the query uses COALESCE on the column
questions.why: For grouping, DISTINCT and UNION, SQL treats NULLs as not distinct from each other, so they form one group. That is different from `=`, where NULL = NULL is unknown. Label the group with `COALESCE(region, 'Unknown')` in reports.
questions.asked: It tests whether you know that grouping and equality treat NULL differently.

questions.q: `ORDER BY last_login ASC` on a nullable column. Where do the NULL rows appear by default?
choices: Last in Postgres; first in SQL Server, MySQL and SQLite
First in every engine, as NULL sorts below all values
Last in every engine, as NULL sorts above all values
In an unspecified position, as NULLs have no defined sort order
questions.why: Postgres treats NULL as larger than any value, so it sorts last ascending; SQL Server, MySQL and SQLite treat it as smallest. Postgres and SQLite accept `NULLS FIRST` / `NULLS LAST`; in SQL Server sort on `CASE WHEN last_login IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END` first.
questions.asked: Engine differences in NULL ordering break paginated lists after a migration; knowing NULLS LAST shows real cross-engine experience.

questions.q: In Postgres or SQL Server, why does this fail?
choices: Arithmetic is not allowed in the SELECT list alongside a WHERE
WHERE runs before SELECT, so the alias does not exist there yet
Aliases must be quoted in double quotes to be used in WHERE
A comparison against a computed column must go in a HAVING clause
questions.why: Logically, FROM and WHERE are evaluated before SELECT, so the alias is unknown in WHERE. Repeat the expression, or wrap the query in a subquery or CTE. ORDER BY runs after SELECT, which is why aliases work there. MySQL allows aliases in HAVING and SQLite even in WHERE, which hides this habit.
questions.asked: It checks you know the logical order of evaluation, which explains a whole family of 'why can't I use that here' errors.

questions.q: How do you count paid and refunded orders per customer in a single pass over `orders`?
choices: COUNT(status = 'paid') and COUNT(status = 'refunded'), grouped by customer_id
SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), and the same for 'refunded'
COUNT(*) with WHERE status IN ('paid', 'refunded'), grouped by customer_id
COUNT(*) with HAVING status IN ('paid', 'refunded'), grouped by customer_id
questions.why: Conditional aggregation puts a CASE inside the aggregate, so each row adds 1 to the column it belongs to. `COUNT(status = 'paid')` counts every row where the comparison is non-NULL, true or false. Postgres and SQLite also offer `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid')`.
questions.asked: Pivot-style reports come up constantly; conditional aggregation is the portable answer interviewers look for.

questions.q: In Postgres, SQL Server or SQLite, `s` holds 'a', 'b' and NULL. How many rows does `WHERE s <> 'a'` keep?
choices: Two, because NULL is different from 'a' and so passes
Three, because <> ignores the NULL and keeps the row
Zero, because a NULL in the column fails the whole scan
One, because NULL <> 'a' is unknown and WHERE drops it
questions.why: Any comparison with NULL yields unknown, and WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true. To include rows with no value, write `s <> 'a' OR s IS NULL`, or `s IS DISTINCT FROM 'a'` in Postgres and SQL Server 2022.
questions.asked: 'Everything except X' filters quietly losing NULL rows is a real bug; the fix shows you think about missing data.

questions.q: What do `5 / 2` and `5 / 2.0` return in Postgres, SQL Server and SQLite?
choices: 2.5 and 2.5, as division always produces a decimal result
3 and 2.5, as integer division rounds to the nearest whole
2 and 2.5, as dividing two integers truncates toward zero
2 and 2, as the left operand's type decides the result
questions.why: Integer divided by integer is integer division in these engines, so percentages computed as `paid / total` come out as 0. Cast one side, for example `paid * 1.0 / total` or `CAST(paid AS numeric)`. MySQL is the odd one out: its `/` returns 2.5000 and `DIV` truncates.
questions.asked: The 'every percentage is zero' bug is common in reporting queries; the cast fix is expected.

questions.q: In Postgres or SQLite, what do `'a' || NULL` and `CONCAT('a', NULL)` return?
choices: NULL and 'a': the operator propagates NULL, CONCAT skips it
'a' and 'a': both treat NULL as an empty string
NULL and NULL: any NULL input makes a string function NULL
'aNULL' and 'a': the operator prints NULL as a literal word
questions.why: The `||` operator follows the NULL-in, NULL-out rule, so a full name built as `first || ' ' || middle || ' ' || last` vanishes when middle is NULL. `CONCAT` treats NULL as empty. SQL Server's `+` on strings also returns NULL, and its `CONCAT` behaves the same way.
questions.asked: Disappearing display names are a classic NULL bug; the answer shows you know which functions propagate NULL.

questions.q: What does this return when `status` is NULL?
questions.code:
SELECT CASE status
  WHEN NULL THEN 'missing'
  ELSE 'present'
END
FROM orders;
choices: 'missing', because the simple CASE has a NULL branch
'present', because status = NULL is never true
NULL, because CASE propagates a NULL input
An error, because NULL is not allowed in WHEN
questions.why: A simple CASE compares with `=`, and `NULL = NULL` is unknown, so the branch never matches and ELSE wins. Use the searched form, `CASE WHEN status IS NULL THEN 'missing' ...`, to test for NULL.
questions.asked: A compact NULL-semantics check; a strong candidate names the searched CASE form as the fix.

questions.q: How do you return the first 10 rows by `created_at` in Postgres, SQL Server and MySQL respectively?
choices: LIMIT 10 in all three, as it is part of the SQL standard
TOP 10; LIMIT 10; FETCH FIRST 10 ROWS ONLY
LIMIT 10; TOP 10 (or OFFSET/FETCH); LIMIT 10
ROWNUM <= 10; TOP 10; LIMIT 10 in a WHERE clause
questions.why: Postgres, MySQL and SQLite use LIMIT (and OFFSET). SQL Server uses `SELECT TOP 10` or `ORDER BY ... OFFSET 0 ROWS FETCH NEXT 10 ROWS ONLY`, and Postgres also accepts the standard FETCH FIRST. ROWNUM is Oracle's older idiom. Any of them without ORDER BY returns an arbitrary 10.
questions.asked: Cheap to ask and quickly shows which engines you have actually used.

questions.q: What does `SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, status FROM orders` remove?
choices: Rows repeating a customer_id, keeping each customer's first status
Rows where customer_id or status is NULL, before comparing
Rows whose status appears for more than one customer
Rows identical in both columns, leaving unique pairs
questions.why: DISTINCT applies to the whole selected row, not the first column, so a customer appears once per distinct status. To pick one row per customer you need GROUP BY with aggregates, a window function, or Postgres's `DISTINCT ON`.
questions.asked: Misreading DISTINCT as 'distinct on the first column' is common; this checks the mental model.

questions.q: In Postgres, what happens when this runs and some customer has two addresses?
questions.code:
SELECT c.name,
  (SELECT a.city FROM addresses a
   WHERE a.customer_id = c.id) AS city
FROM customers c;
choices: The row for that customer repeats once per address
The address inserted first is used for that customer
The two cities are concatenated into one comma-separated value
The query fails: a subquery returned more than one row
questions.why: A subquery in the SELECT list must be scalar: at most one row, one column. With two rows it errors at run time (SQL Server does the same). It returns NULL when there are no rows. Decide which address you mean, with ORDER BY and LIMIT 1, or join and aggregate.
questions.asked: Scalar subqueries that work in dev and fail on real data are a familiar production error.

questions.q: Which rule applies to the two SELECTs in a UNION?
choices: They must have the same column count and compatible types; names come from the first
They must select from the same table, or from tables that share an identical schema
They must use identical column names, or the second query's names are used
They may differ in column count; any missing columns are padded out with NULL values
questions.why: UNION matches columns by position, so both sides need the same number of columns with compatible types, and the result takes its column names from the first query. An ORDER BY applies to the combined result and goes at the very end.
questions.asked: Asked with a broken UNION to fix; matching by position rather than name is the key insight.

questions.q: In Postgres, SQL Server or SQLite, which returns the ids in `import_batch` that are not already in `products`?
choices: SELECT id FROM import_batch INTERSECT SELECT id FROM products
SELECT id FROM import_batch UNION SELECT id FROM products
SELECT id FROM import_batch EXCEPT SELECT id FROM products
SELECT id FROM products EXCEPT SELECT id FROM import_batch
questions.why: `A EXCEPT B` returns the distinct rows of A that are not in B; the order matters, so the last option returns products missing from the batch. INTERSECT returns rows in both. Oracle spells EXCEPT as MINUS, and unlike NOT IN it treats NULLs as equal.
questions.asked: Set operators are a quick way to answer 'what's new or missing' in data migrations; interviewers like seeing them used.

questions.q: In Postgres, what does this return for a customer with no orders?
questions.code:
SELECT c.name,
  (SELECT MAX(o.created_at) FROM orders o
   WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) AS last_order
FROM customers c;
choices: The customer is left out of the result
The customer's row, with last_order NULL
An error, because MAX saw no input rows
The customer's row, with last_order set to the epoch
questions.why: The outer query drives the rows, so every customer appears; the scalar subquery returns MAX over no rows, which is NULL. A correlated subquery like this runs per customer in principle, but planners often rewrite it into a join; check the plan for large tables.
questions.asked: It checks you can reason about correlated subqueries rather than only joins.

questions.q: `RIGHT JOIN` shows up in a query you are reviewing. How does `a RIGHT JOIN b ON ...` relate to a LEFT JOIN?
choices: It keeps only rows of b that have no match in a, the reverse of an anti-join
It returns the same rows as `b LEFT JOIN a ON ...`, just with a's columns first
It keeps every row of both a and b, filling in NULLs on whichever side has no match
It is faster than a LEFT JOIN when b is the larger of the two tables
questions.why: A RIGHT JOIN keeps every row of the right table; swapping the tables and using LEFT gives the same result. Most teams write only LEFT JOINs so the 'kept' table always reads first. Keeping every row of both is FULL OUTER JOIN.
questions.asked: A simple clarity question; saying you would rewrite it as a LEFT JOIN is the answer reviewers like.

questions.q: Rows in `orders` and `refunds` both have a nullable `coupon_code`. Why does a join on `o.coupon_code = r.coupon_code` never pair two rows that both have NULL?
choices: Joins skip NULL keys only when the column is part of an index
NULL = NULL is unknown, and a join keeps only true matches
The planner removes NULL rows before a hash join, but not a merge join
The rows do pair, but the output shows the key column as NULL
questions.why: Join conditions use ordinary equality, so NULL never matches NULL whatever the join algorithm. If 'both missing' should match, write `o.coupon_code IS NOT DISTINCT FROM r.coupon_code` (Postgres, SQL Server 2022), or rethink whether NULL is the right model.
questions.asked: It checks you apply NULL rules to joins, where they cause 'missing row' bugs in reconciliation.

questions.q: In SQL Server, `@code` is `varchar(3)` and NULL. What does `ISNULL(@code, 'UNKNOWN')` return?
choices: 'UNKNOWN', exactly as COALESCE would, as the types are compatible
NULL, because ISNULL only replaces empty strings
An error, because the replacement is too long
'UNK', because ISNULL takes the first argument's type
questions.why: ISNULL's result type is the type of its first argument, so the replacement is silently truncated to three characters. COALESCE follows data-type precedence across all arguments and returns 'UNKNOWN'. It is one reason to prefer the standard COALESCE.
questions.asked: A SQL Server gotcha that shows real experience; the strong answer is 'use COALESCE unless you have a reason'.

questions.q: Which condition is true when both `a` and `b` are NULL, and false when exactly one of them is?
choices: a = b OR a IS NULL
a IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b
COALESCE(a, 0) = COALESCE(b, 0)
NOT (a <> b)
questions.why: `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` is a null-safe equality: it treats two NULLs as equal and never returns unknown. It is supported in Postgres, SQL Server 2022 and SQLite (as `IS`); MySQL spells it `<=>`. `a = b` and `NOT (a <> b)` are unknown when either side is NULL, and a COALESCE sentinel wrongly matches a real 0.
questions.asked: Useful for 'has this value changed?' checks in upserts and audits; knowing the operator saves a messy OR chain.

questions.q: How does `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)` behave for a customer with 500 orders?
choices: It builds a list of all 500 order ids, then tests it for emptiness
It counts the 500 orders and compares the count with zero
It returns true and may stop at the first matching order
It returns 500 true rows, which the outer query collapses
questions.why: EXISTS is a semi-join: it only asks whether any row matches, so the engine can stop at the first one, and the selected columns do not matter. `COUNT(*) > 0` asks the database to count every match first, which does more work for the same answer.
questions.asked: It shows you pick EXISTS over COUNT(*) > 0 for 'does any row exist', a small but real performance habit.

questions.q: You run `SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY 2 DESC`. What does `ORDER BY 2` mean?
choices: Sort by the second column of the table, whatever the SELECT list
Sort by the second column of the SELECT list, here the count
Sort by the constant value 2, so the order is left unchanged
Return only the first two groups, in descending order
questions.why: A number in ORDER BY refers to a position in the SELECT list. It is handy in ad-hoc queries but fragile in code, because adding a column shifts the meaning; naming the alias is clearer. Positional GROUP BY works in Postgres and MySQL but not SQL Server.
questions.asked: A small readability question; the good answer mentions why you avoid positional ordering in application SQL.

questions.q: Which query returns the customers whose total spend is above the average customer's total spend?
choices: WHERE SUM(total) > AVG(total), followed by GROUP BY customer_id
GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(total) > AVG(total), in one query
HAVING SUM(total) > the average of per-customer sums, from a CTE
HAVING SUM(total) > (SELECT AVG(total) FROM orders), in a subquery
questions.why: You need the average of per-customer totals, which is an aggregate of an aggregate, so it lives in a CTE or subquery. `HAVING SUM(total) > AVG(total)` compares each customer's sum with their own average order, and `AVG(total)` over all orders is the average order, not the average customer. Aggregates in WHERE are an error.
questions.asked: Nested aggregation separates people who can reason about grain from those who pattern-match HAVING.

questions.q: What does declaring a column as the PRIMARY KEY give you, in Postgres, SQL Server and MySQL alike?
choices: Uniqueness only; NULLs are still allowed, and you add an index yourself
An auto-incrementing value, whatever the column's declared type
Uniqueness and NOT NULL, enforced through an index the engine creates
A foreign key that every other table must reference, by convention
questions.why: A primary key is unique and not null, and every mainstream engine backs it with a unique index (clustered by default in SQL Server and InnoDB). Auto-increment is separate: IDENTITY, a sequence or AUTO_INCREMENT. SQLite is the historical exception, allowing NULLs in some non-integer primary keys.
questions.asked: A basic check that you know what the database enforces for you versus what is convention.

questions.q: `users.email` has a plain UNIQUE constraint and is nullable. Two users sign up without an email. What happens?
choices: The two inserts succeed in Postgres, MySQL and SQLite; SQL Server rejects the second NULL
The two inserts succeed everywhere, because a NULL is never checked for uniqueness
The second insert fails in every engine, as two NULLs count as duplicate values
The two inserts fail in Postgres, because a UNIQUE column implies it is NOT NULL
questions.why: The standard treats NULLs as distinct, so Postgres, MySQL and SQLite allow many. SQL Server's unique constraint allows only one NULL; use a filtered unique index `WHERE email IS NOT NULL` there. Postgres 15+ can opt into the stricter rule with `UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT`.
questions.asked: Optional-but-unique columns are common, and this engine difference bites when a schema moves between databases.

questions.q: `status` is `NOT NULL DEFAULT 'new'` and `note` is `DEFAULT 'x'`. What does `INSERT INTO t (id, note) VALUES (2, NULL)` store?
choices: status 'new' and note 'x', as defaults replace any NULL that is supplied
An error, as the explicit NULL in note conflicts with note's default
status NULL and note NULL, as a default only fills the first column
status 'new' and note NULL, as a default fills only an omitted column
questions.why: A default is used when the column is left out of the INSERT (or given the keyword DEFAULT). An explicit NULL is a value, so note becomes NULL. If the column should never be empty, the default is not enough: add NOT NULL, as status has.
questions.asked: ORMs sending explicit NULLs for unset properties is a common reason defaults 'don't work'.

questions.q: You want to guarantee a product's price is never negative, whatever code writes to the table. What is the most direct tool?
choices: A validation attribute on the API model, as every write goes through the API
A CHECK constraint such as CHECK (price >= 0) on the column
An AFTER INSERT trigger that deletes any row with a negative price
A view over the table that filters out rows with a negative price
questions.why: A CHECK constraint is evaluated on every insert and update, from any client, and rejects the bad row. Keep the API validation too, for friendly messages, but it does not cover scripts, other services or ad-hoc fixes. A cleanup trigger lets the bad row exist and hides the error.
questions.asked: Checks whether you let the database enforce invariants instead of trusting every writer.

questions.q: In the sqlite3 CLI (or a driver with default settings), this table has a REFERENCES clause. Why might an order pointing at a missing customer still insert?
choices: SQLite enforces foreign keys only on columns that also carry an index
SQLite checks foreign keys only when the transaction commits
Foreign keys are off per connection until PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON
SQLite ignores REFERENCES clauses unless the table is declared STRICT
questions.why: For backward compatibility, SQLite parses foreign keys but enforces them only on connections that run `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON`. Many wrappers switch it on (Node's built-in node:sqlite does), but not all, so set it explicitly on every connection. STRICT tables enforce column types, not foreign keys.
questions.asked: SQLite is common in tests and small apps; this gotcha shows you have actually shipped with it.

questions.q: `orders.coupon_id` references `coupons(id)` with `ON DELETE SET NULL`. What happens to orders when a coupon is deleted?
choices: They are deleted along with the coupon, as with CASCADE
Their coupon_id becomes NULL, and the orders are kept
The delete fails while any order still uses the coupon
They keep the old id, now pointing at a missing coupon
questions.why: SET NULL clears the reference and keeps the child row, which suits optional links such as a coupon. The default (NO ACTION or RESTRICT) blocks the delete, and CASCADE removes the children. The column must be nullable for SET NULL to work.
questions.asked: It checks you choose delete behaviour per relationship rather than cascading everything.

questions.q: In Postgres or SQL Server, a transaction inserts an order, receives id 101, then rolls back. What id does the next successful insert get?
choices: 101, because the rolled-back value is returned to the sequence
The lowest unused id in the table, found by scanning for gaps
An error until the sequence is reset to the last committed value
102, because sequence values are not reused, so ids have gaps
questions.why: Sequences and IDENTITY hand out numbers outside the transaction so that concurrent inserts never wait on each other; a rollback does not return the number. Gaps are normal, so never use ids as a count or as a gap-free invoice number.
questions.asked: Asked when someone wants 'no gaps' invoice numbers; knowing why ids have gaps shows you understand concurrency trade-offs.

questions.q: After inserting a row, how should the application get its generated id?
choices: Run SELECT MAX(id) FROM the table straight after the insert
Use RETURNING id (Postgres, SQLite) or OUTPUT INSERTED.id (SQL Server)
Generate the next id in the application by adding one to the last id it saw
Query the row back by all its other columns and read its id
questions.why: RETURNING and OUTPUT hand back the value produced by this statement, in the same round trip, and are safe under concurrency. `MAX(id)` can return another session's row. MySQL uses `LAST_INSERT_ID()`, and SQL Server's `SCOPE_IDENTITY()` is the older equivalent.
questions.asked: The MAX(id) race is a classic junior mistake; the engine-specific answer shows hands-on experience.

questions.q: Why can random UUIDv4 primary keys slow down inserts on a large table in SQL Server or InnoDB, and what is the usual remedy?
choices: UUIDs are compared as strings; storing them as text avoids that cost
Random keys land all over the clustered index; use UUIDv7 or a bigint
UUIDs cannot be indexed, so each insert scans the table for duplicates
Every UUID is generated by the server; generating it in the app fixes it
questions.why: Inserts into a clustered index at random positions split pages and touch far more of the index than appending at the end, and the index grows bigger and fragmented. Time-ordered UUIDv7 (native `uuidv7()` in Postgres 18) or a sequential id keeps inserts at the end while staying globally unique.
questions.asked: Key choice comes up in design interviews; knowing why random keys hurt a B-tree shows depth.

questions.q: In Postgres, what is the practical difference between `varchar(255)` and `text`?
choices: text is stored outside the row, so it is always slower to read
varchar(255) is faster, as the engine can reserve a fixed width
Only the length check; both are stored and processed identically
text cannot be indexed in a B-tree, so varchar is needed for any lookups
questions.why: In Postgres, varchar(n) is text plus a length check; storage and speed are the same, and long values of either type are moved out of line (TOASTed) automatically. Use a length limit when it is a real rule, or a CHECK constraint, rather than 255 by habit. SQL Server differs: nvarchar(max) has real costs.
questions.asked: It reveals whether you carry MySQL or SQL Server habits into Postgres without knowing why.

questions.q: In SQL Server, why store customer names in `nvarchar` rather than `varchar` on a database with a default Latin collation?
choices: varchar there cannot hold characters outside the code page, such as Chinese
nvarchar values are compressed, so they use less space than varchar
varchar columns cannot be indexed when they are longer than 50 characters
nvarchar always sorts case-sensitively, which names need for correct lookups
questions.why: With a legacy code-page collation, varchar holds one code page and turns other characters into '?'. nvarchar stores UTF-16 and holds any character. SQL Server 2019+ also offers UTF-8 collations for varchar. Pass parameters as nvarchar too, or string literals need the N prefix: N'Zoë'.
questions.asked: Question marks in customer names are a real support ticket; this checks you know the cause.

questions.q: What range can a column declared `DECIMAL(10, 2)` hold?
choices: Up to 10 digits before the decimal point and 2 digits after it
Up to 99,999,999.99: 10 digits in total, 2 after the point
Any value, rounded to 10 significant figures on insert
Up to 10.2 million, as the precision counts in millions
questions.why: Precision is the total number of digits and scale is the number after the decimal point, so 8 remain before it. Values with more decimal places are rounded, and values too large are rejected with an overflow error rather than silently clamped.
questions.asked: Precision and scale confusion causes overflow errors on real prices and totals.

questions.q: `WHERE name = 'ann'` finds 'Ann' on SQL Server but not on Postgres. Why?
choices: SQL Server lowercases all string literals before it compares them
Postgres needs double quotes around a string for it to match
SQL Server's usual default collation is case-insensitive; Postgres compares exactly
Postgres indexes store only uppercased copies of every string value they hold
questions.why: Comparison rules come from the collation. SQL Server installs usually default to a case-insensitive collation such as SQL_Latin1_General_CP1_CI_AS; Postgres compares case-sensitively by default. In Postgres use `lower(name) = lower($1)` with an expression index, `citext`, or a nondeterministic ICU collation.
questions.asked: Case-insensitive login lookups break when moving between engines; this is a practical portability question.

questions.q: What does `WHERE code LIKE 'A_1'` match?
choices: Only the literal string 'A_1', underscore included
Any code starting with A and ending with 1, of any length
Any three-character code with A first and 1 last
Codes starting with 'A' followed by one or more 1s
questions.why: In LIKE, `_` matches exactly one character and `%` matches any run, including none. To match a literal underscore, escape it: `LIKE 'A\_1' ESCAPE '\'` (or `[_]` in SQL Server). Codes containing underscores silently over-match otherwise.
questions.asked: Wildcard escaping comes up in search features; the ESCAPE clause is the detail interviewers listen for.

questions.q: A search box builds `WHERE name LIKE $1` with the parameter `'%' + input + '%'`. A user types `%`. What happens?
choices: Injection: the % is executed as SQL and the query text is changed
The query fails, because % cannot appear inside a bound parameter
Nothing unusual; bound parameters escape LIKE wildcards as well as quotes
The search matches every row, as parameters do not escape wildcards
questions.why: A parameter keeps input out of the SQL text, so this is not injection, but inside the value `%` and `_` are still LIKE wildcards. Escape them in the app and add an ESCAPE clause if users should be able to search for them literally. A search for `%` returning everything can also be a performance problem on large tables.
questions.asked: It separates 'parameters prevent injection' from 'parameters make input inert', a nuance strong candidates know.

questions.q: An endpoint lets the client choose the sort column. Why can you not simply bind it as a parameter in `ORDER BY $1`?
choices: Parameters carry values, not identifiers; map the input to an allowlist of columns
You can, but binding identifiers is slower, so string-concatenating is preferred
ORDER BY does not accept any expressions, so the column must be hard-coded
Parameters only work in WHERE clauses, so ORDER BY must go through a stored procedure
questions.why: A bound value is treated as a constant, so `ORDER BY $1` sorts every row by the same literal string and does nothing useful (or errors). Identifiers cannot be parameters. Map the client's choice to a fixed set of column names in code, never interpolating raw input.
questions.asked: Dynamic sorting is where parameterised-query discipline usually breaks; the allowlist answer is what reviewers expect.

questions.q: In Postgres with node-postgres, how do you pass a variable-length list of ids safely to a query?
questions.code:
const ids = [3, 9, 27];
await pool.query(/* ? */, [ids]);
choices: 'SELECT * FROM users WHERE id IN ($1)', which expands the array into a list
'SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ANY($1)', binding the array as one parameter
'SELECT * FROM users WHERE id IN (' + ids.join(',') + ')', since ids are numbers
'SELECT * FROM users WHERE id IN $1', which node-postgres turns into a tuple
questions.why: Postgres accepts an array parameter, and `= ANY($1)` tests membership, with one plan for any list length. `IN ($1)` compares id with the whole array and fails. Concatenating 'safe' numbers is a habit that breaks the day the list comes from a query string. In SQL Server, use a table-valued parameter or one parameter per item.
questions.asked: Filtering by a list of ids is everyday work; the ANY pattern shows Postgres fluency.

questions.q: In Postgres with no explicit BEGIN, you run two UPDATE statements from a client and the second fails. What state is the first update in?
choices: Committed, because each statement ran in its own implicit transaction
Rolled back, because the session undoes everything since it connected
Pending, because it waits for an explicit COMMIT from the client
Rolled back, because the second failure aborts the whole batch
questions.why: Clients default to autocommit: every statement outside an explicit transaction is committed on its own. To make the two changes all-or-nothing, wrap them in BEGIN ... COMMIT (or your driver's transaction API). SQL Server behaves the same unless IMPLICIT_TRANSACTIONS is on.
questions.asked: Partial updates after an error are how people learn about autocommit; this checks you already know.

questions.q: Inside a Postgres transaction, an INSERT fails on a unique constraint. The code catches the error and runs another SELECT in the same transaction. What happens?
choices: The SELECT runs normally, and COMMIT keeps the other statements
The SELECT runs, but COMMIT silently commits only the SELECT
The SELECT fails: the transaction is aborted until you roll back
The failed INSERT is retried automatically before the SELECT is allowed to run
questions.why: After an error, Postgres marks the transaction aborted and rejects every further command ('current transaction is aborted') until ROLLBACK; a COMMIT then acts as a rollback. To recover from an expected error mid-transaction, set a SAVEPOINT before it and roll back to it. SQL Server, by contrast, often continues unless XACT_ABORT is on.
questions.asked: The 'current transaction is aborted' error confuses many developers; explaining it shows real Postgres experience.

questions.q: What is a SAVEPOINT useful for inside a transaction?
choices: Committing part of the work early while the transaction continues
Rolling back to a marked point and continuing, without losing earlier work
Making the transaction's changes visible to other sessions ahead of commit
Raising the isolation level for the statements that follow the savepoint
questions.why: `ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT x` undoes only what happened after x, and the transaction carries on; nothing is committed or visible to others until the final COMMIT. ORMs use savepoints for nested transactions, and they are how you try an insert that may conflict without aborting the whole unit.
questions.asked: Nested transactions in ORMs are implemented with savepoints; knowing that explains otherwise puzzling behaviour.

questions.q: In Postgres, you add a foreign key `orders.customer_id REFERENCES customers(id)`. What index work does that do for you?
choices: It indexes orders.customer_id automatically, as MySQL InnoDB does
None; the referenced key is already indexed, the referencing column is not
It indexes both columns and clusters orders by customer_id
It creates a hash index on customer_id, which serves equality lookups only
questions.why: Postgres and SQL Server require a unique index on the referenced key but do not index the referencing column; InnoDB does. Without one, joins from customers to orders and every customer delete (which must check for children) scan orders. Add the index yourself.
questions.asked: Missing FK indexes are one of the most common real performance problems; this checks you know to add them.

questions.q: Is a single-column index on `is_active` (true for 98% of rows) likely to speed up `WHERE is_active = true`?
choices: Yes, every column used in a WHERE clause should get an index
Yes, but only when the index is declared UNIQUE, so each lookup stops early
No, as boolean columns can never be included in an index
No, as the filter keeps most rows, so a table scan is cheaper
questions.why: An index pays off when it narrows the search to a small fraction of rows. Reading 98% of a table through an index costs more than scanning it. The rare value (inactive rows) might benefit, and a partial index `WHERE is_active = false` keeps that small.
questions.asked: 'Index everything in the WHERE' is a junior instinct; selectivity is the concept interviewers want.

questions.q: What is the difference between a view and a materialised view (Postgres; an indexed view in SQL Server)?
choices: A view is a stored query run on each use; a materialised view stores results
A view is read-only; a materialised view accepts inserts and updates
A view exists only for the current session; a materialised view persists for all
A view can join tables; a materialised view reads from one table
questions.why: A plain view is a named query that is expanded into each query that uses it, so it is always current and costs the same as the query. A materialised view stores the result and must be refreshed (`REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW`), trading freshness for speed; SQL Server's indexed views are maintained on every write instead.
questions.asked: Asked when discussing slow dashboards; the freshness trade-off is the part that matters.

questions.q: You must run a one-off `UPDATE` in production to fix some rows. What is the safest habit?
choices: Run it quickly outside any transaction so that locks are held briefly
Run it in a transaction, check the affected row count, then commit
Copy the whole table first with SELECT INTO, then run the update
Disable the table's triggers and constraints first so it cannot fail
questions.why: Wrapping the change in BEGIN lets you compare the affected row count (and a SELECT of the result) with what you expected, then COMMIT or ROLLBACK. Test the WHERE clause as a SELECT first. Keep the transaction short so locks are not held while you think.
questions.asked: Everyone has a story about an UPDATE without a WHERE; interviewers want to hear the habit that prevents it.

questions.q: How do you update `orders.region` from the matching `customers.region`, in Postgres and SQL Server respectively?
choices: Postgres: UPDATE orders o JOIN customers c ON ...; SQL Server: UPDATE ... USING customers
Both: UPDATE orders SET region = customers.region, as the join is inferred from the FK
Postgres: UPDATE orders SET ... FROM customers c WHERE ...; SQL Server: UPDATE o SET ... FROM orders o JOIN customers c
Neither engine can join inside an UPDATE, so you loop over customers and update orders one at a time
questions.why: Postgres adds the other table with FROM and joins it in WHERE; SQL Server names the alias after UPDATE and joins in FROM; MySQL writes `UPDATE orders o JOIN customers c ON ... SET ...`. For deletes, Postgres uses `DELETE ... USING`. A set-based statement beats looping row by row.
questions.asked: Set-based updates across tables are routine data fixes; the syntax differences catch people out.

questions.q: Dates are stored as text like '2026-9-30' and '2026-10-01'. Why does `ORDER BY created` put October before September?
choices: Text columns sort in insertion order when no index covers them
The engine parses the text as dates, but guesses the wrong format
Text sorts by character, and '1' comes before '9' at that point
Sorting text always places longer strings ahead of shorter ones
questions.why: Text is compared character by character, so '2026-10' sorts before '2026-9'. Zero-padded ISO 8601 strings do sort correctly, which is why SQLite apps get away with text dates, but a real date or timestamp type also validates values and supports date arithmetic.
questions.asked: A simple way to check you use real date types and understand why ISO format matters when you cannot.

questions.q: In Postgres, how do you count orders per calendar day?
choices: GROUP BY created_at, which the engine rounds to the day
GROUP BY date_trunc('day', created_at), or created_at::date
GROUP BY DAY(created_at), which returns the full date
GROUP BY created_at, with a HAVING clause keeping only midnight
questions.why: Truncate the timestamp to the day and group on that. With timestamptz, 'which day' depends on the time zone, so convert first, for example `(created_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/London')::date`. `DAY()` in SQL Server and MySQL returns only the day of the month, 1 to 31, merging different months.
questions.asked: Daily-count reports are routine; the time-zone caveat is what makes the answer strong.

questions.q: Page 5,000 of a product list uses `ORDER BY id LIMIT 20 OFFSET 99980` and is slow. Why?
choices: OFFSET forces a full sort of the table, even when id is indexed
The database must still read and discard all 99,980 rows before the page
OFFSET disables every index, so the query falls back to a table scan
Large OFFSET values are cached less, so each request misses the buffer cache and reads disk
questions.why: OFFSET is implemented by producing the skipped rows and throwing them away, so cost grows with the page number even when an index supplies them in order. Keyset pagination (`WHERE id > last_seen ORDER BY id LIMIT 20`) jumps straight to the page through the index.
questions.asked: Explaining why OFFSET degrades is the setup for recommending keyset pagination in API design interviews.

questions.q: How do you add a NOT NULL constraint to an existing column that already contains some NULLs?
choices: Just add it; existing NULLs are converted to the column default
Just add it; it applies only to rows inserted from now on
Backfill the NULLs with real values first, then add the constraint
Drop the column and re-create it with NOT NULL, as it cannot change
questions.why: Adding NOT NULL validates existing rows and fails if any are NULL, so fix the data first with an UPDATE. On big live tables do the backfill in batches. In Postgres 12+ you can add a validated `CHECK (col IS NOT NULL)` first, which lets SET NOT NULL skip its own full scan.
questions.asked: Tightening a schema on existing data is everyday migration work; this checks you expect the validation.

questions.q: Why prefer a unique constraint over a unique index when the rule is part of the data model?
choices: A unique constraint is enforced at commit, while an index checks nothing
A unique index cannot span more than a single column of the table
A constraint states intent and can be a foreign key target; enforcement is the same
Only constraints are enforced under concurrency; a unique index can let concurrent duplicates in
questions.why: Engines implement a unique constraint with a unique index, so enforcement is identical. The constraint documents a business rule, shows up in schema tools, and can be referenced by foreign keys in all engines. A unique index lets you add things constraints cannot, such as a WHERE clause or expressions.
questions.asked: A nuance question: knowing both enforce the same way, and when you need the index form, shows you know the engine internals.

questions.q: `products` has prices 9, 10, 15, 20 and 21. Which prices does `WHERE price BETWEEN 10 AND 20` keep?
choices: 15 only, because both end values are excluded
10 and 15, because the upper end value is excluded
10, 15 and 20, because both ends are included
15 and 20, because the lower end value is excluded
questions.why: `BETWEEN a AND b` means `>= a AND <= b` in every mainstream engine. That inclusive upper bound is why it is a trap for timestamps: `BETWEEN '2026-03-01' AND '2026-03-31'` misses most of 31 March, so half-open ranges (`>= start AND < next`) are safer there.
questions.asked: It is basic, but the follow-up about dates shows whether you have been bitten by the inclusive end.

questions.q: `users` holds (Smith, Al), (Jones, Bo), (Smith, Cy). What order does this return?
