questions.code:
SELECT last_name, first_name FROM users
ORDER BY last_name, first_name DESC;
choices: Smith Cy, Smith Al, Jones Bo
Jones Bo, Smith Al, Smith Cy
Smith Al, Smith Cy, Jones Bo
Jones Bo, Smith Cy, Smith Al
questions.why: Each ORDER BY key has its own direction, and the default is ASC, so last_name sorts ascending and DESC applies only to first_name as the tiebreaker. Writing DESC once at the end does not flip every column.
questions.asked: Multi-column sorts are in every list endpoint, and misreading DESC's scope is a frequent bug.

questions.q: What does `COALESCE(nickname, first_name, 'Guest')` return for a user whose nickname is NULL and first_name is 'Ann'?
choices: 'Ann', the first non-NULL argument
NULL, because one argument is NULL
'Guest', the final fallback value
'Ann Guest', joined from the non-NULLs
questions.why: COALESCE returns its first argument that is not NULL, reading left to right, so it only falls through to 'Guest' when both columns are NULL. It is standard SQL across Postgres, SQL Server, MySQL and SQLite, and it never concatenates.
questions.asked: Defaulting NULLs for display or maths is daily work, and COALESCE is the portable tool.

questions.q: What does this return for a score of 75?
questions.code:
SELECT CASE
  WHEN score >= 50 THEN 'pass'
  WHEN score >= 70 THEN 'merit'
  ELSE 'fail'
END AS grade;
choices: 'merit', because it is the more specific match
'pass', because the first true branch wins
'pass merit', because both branches are true
An error, because two branches overlap
questions.why: A searched CASE evaluates WHEN branches top to bottom and stops at the first true one, so the stricter test must come first. Overlapping conditions are legal and produce no warning, which is exactly why this bug survives review.
questions.asked: Bucketing values with CASE is common in reports, and branch order is the classic mistake.

questions.q: Which query lists email addresses that appear on more than one row of `users`?
choices: SELECT email FROM users WHERE COUNT(*) > 1 GROUP BY email;
SELECT DISTINCT email FROM users WHERE email IS NOT UNIQUE;
SELECT email FROM users GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
SELECT email, COUNT(*) FROM users ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 1;
questions.why: Grouping by email collapses duplicates, and HAVING filters on the aggregate after grouping. WHERE runs before grouping so it cannot see COUNT(*), and the LIMIT 1 version returns only the single most common email, even if it is unique.
questions.asked: Finding duplicates before adding a unique constraint is a real migration task, not a puzzle.

questions.q: Ana has two orders and Ben has none. What do `a` and `b` show for Ben?
questions.code:
SELECT c.name, COUNT(*) AS a, COUNT(o.id) AS b
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;
choices: a = 0 and b = 0
a = 1 and b = 1
a = 0 and b = 1
a = 1 and b = 0
questions.why: The LEFT JOIN keeps Ben as one row with NULL order columns, so `COUNT(*)` counts that row (1) while `COUNT(o.id)` skips the NULL (0). Always count a column from the optional side when counting children.
questions.asked: 'Orders per customer including zero' is a common request, and COUNT(*) here is a subtle wrong-number bug.

questions.q: How do you copy last year's rows from `orders` into `orders_archive`, which has the same columns?
choices: INSERT INTO orders_archive SELECT * FROM orders WHERE created_at < '2026-01-01';
INSERT INTO orders_archive VALUES (SELECT * FROM orders WHERE created_at < '2026-01-01');
SELECT * INTO orders WHERE created_at < '2026-01-01' FROM orders_archive;
COPY orders TO orders_archive WHERE created_at < '2026-01-01';
questions.why: `INSERT INTO target SELECT ...` inserts every row the query returns, set-based in one statement; listing columns explicitly on both sides is safer than `*`. VALUES takes literal rows, not a subquery of many rows, and SQL Server's `SELECT INTO` creates a new table rather than appending.
questions.asked: Set-based copies replace slow row-by-row loops in app code, which interviewers like to see.

questions.q: An API runs `UPDATE products SET price = $1 WHERE id = $2` for an id that does not exist. What happens?
choices: The statement fails with a 'row not found' error
It succeeds and reports 0 rows affected
It inserts a new row with that id and price
It succeeds and reports 1 row affected
questions.why: A WHERE that matches nothing is not an error, so the driver returns a row count of 0; the API must check it and return 404, otherwise the client is told the update worked. Inserting when missing needs an explicit upsert.
questions.asked: Checking rows affected is how update and delete endpoints return correct status codes.

questions.q: In SQL Server, `Code` is `varchar(10)` and a row holds 'ABC  ' (two trailing spaces). What does `WHERE Code = 'ABC'` do?
choices: It does not match, because the stored value is longer
It raises an error, because the lengths are different
It matches, as trailing spaces are ignored by `=`
It matches only if ANSI_PADDING was OFF at creation
questions.why: SQL Server follows the ANSI rule of padding the shorter string with spaces before comparing, so trailing spaces never affect `=` (LIKE does see them). Postgres `text` and `varchar` compare them as real characters, so the same data can match on one engine and not the other.
questions.asked: It explains mysterious duplicate-key errors and lookup mismatches when data moves between engines.

questions.q: Which cut-off expressions select orders from the last 7 days in Postgres and in SQL Server respectively?
choices: PG: now() - 7 * 86400; SQL Server: DATEADD(second, -7, SYSUTCDATETIME())
PG: date('now', '-7 days'); SQL Server: DATEDIFF(day, 7, SYSUTCDATETIME())
PG: DATEADD(day, -7, now()); SQL Server: SYSUTCDATETIME() - interval '7 days'
PG: now() - interval '7 days'; SQL Server: DATEADD(day, -7, SYSUTCDATETIME())
questions.why: Postgres subtracts an interval from a timestamp; SQL Server uses DATEADD, and the UTC function suits UTC-stored data. `date('now', '-7 days')` is SQLite syntax, and DATEDIFF returns a count of boundaries, not a date.
questions.asked: Date arithmetic differs in every engine, and knowing both forms is expected in mixed-stack shops.

questions.q: In SQL Server, `Rating` is an `int` column holding 4 and 5. What does `SELECT AVG(Rating)` return?
choices: 4, because the average is an int
4.5, as a decimal value
5, because the result is rounded
4.50, as a money value
questions.why: SQL Server's AVG returns the same type as its input, so an int column averages with integer division and truncates to 4. Use `AVG(CAST(Rating AS decimal(5,2)))` or `AVG(Rating * 1.0)`. Postgres returns numeric (4.5) for the same query.
questions.asked: Ratings and scores are often ints, and silent truncation ships wrong numbers to dashboards.

questions.q: In SQL Server, `SELECT SUM(Quantity) FROM OrderLines` fails with an arithmetic overflow on a large table, though Quantity values are small. Why?
choices: SUM switches to float after a million rows, which loses precision
SUM over int returns int, which overflows past about 2.1 billion
SUM needs an index on Quantity once the table exceeds its buffer
SUM overflows because NULL quantities are counted as the maximum
questions.why: SQL Server's SUM over int returns int, so a total above 2,147,483,647 overflows even though each value is small. `SUM(CAST(Quantity AS bigint))` fixes it; COUNT has the same issue, hence COUNT_BIG. Postgres widens SUM(int) to bigint automatically.
questions.asked: Reports that worked for years fail as data grows, and this is one of the classic causes.

questions.q: `order_lines` has (price 10, qty 2), (price 5, qty NULL) and (price 3, qty 1). What does `SELECT SUM(price * qty)` return?
choices: NULL, because one line total is NULL
28, treating the NULL quantity as 1
23, because the NULL line total is skipped
An error, because NULL cannot be multiplied
questions.why: Any arithmetic with NULL gives NULL, so the middle line total is NULL, and SUM ignores NULLs, adding 20 + 3. That quietly drops a line from the invoice; `COALESCE(qty, 0)` or a NOT NULL constraint makes the intent explicit.
questions.asked: NULLs silently disappearing from totals is a common money bug.

questions.q: A conversion-rate query divides `orders / visits`, and some days have 0 visits. What does `orders / NULLIF(visits, 0)` do?
choices: Returns zero for those days rather than raising an error
Returns orders unchanged by dividing by 1 instead
Skips those days, removing them from the result set
Returns NULL for those days instead of raising an error
questions.why: NULLIF(x, 0) returns NULL when x is 0, and dividing by NULL yields NULL rather than a divide-by-zero error (which Postgres and SQL Server raise; SQLite already returns NULL). Wrap it in COALESCE if you want 0 displayed; the row stays in the result.
questions.asked: Rate calculations hit zero denominators constantly, and NULLIF is the idiomatic guard.

questions.q: What does `GROUP BY country, city` produce?
choices: One row per distinct combination of country and city
One row per country, with the cities listed inside it
One row per country, then one row per city, stacked
One row per city, merging same-named cities worldwide
questions.why: Grouping by several columns makes a group for each distinct pair, so Paris, France and Paris, Texas stay separate. Subtotals per country as extra rows need ROLLUP or GROUPING SETS.
questions.asked: It checks you picture what a group is before writing report queries.

questions.q: In Postgres 17 or SQL Server 2022, how do `WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)` and the equivalent `WHERE EXISTS (...)` usually compare in speed?
choices: IN is always slower, because it builds the whole list first
They are usually planned identically, as a semi-join
EXISTS is always slower, because it runs once per outer row
IN is faster, because it can use an index but EXISTS cannot
questions.why: Modern optimisers rewrite both into a semi-join and choose hash, merge or nested-loop freely, so the plans usually match. The real difference is NULL handling with NOT IN versus NOT EXISTS, not speed; old advice about IN building a list comes from much older engines.
questions.asked: Interviewers want to see you check the plan instead of repeating folklore.

questions.q: In SQL Server 2022 (or Postgres before 16), why does this fail?
choices: Aggregates cannot be nested across a subquery boundary
COUNT(*) needs an alias only when used inside HAVING
A derived table in FROM must be given an alias
GROUP BY is not allowed inside a subquery in FROM
questions.why: Derived tables must be named, e.g. `) AS per_customer`, in SQL Server, MySQL and Postgres up to 15; Postgres 16 made the alias optional. Averaging the per-customer counts this way is otherwise perfectly valid.
questions.asked: Two-level aggregation (average of counts) is a common report shape and needs a derived table or CTE.

questions.q: Where does the ORDER BY apply in this query?
questions.code:
SELECT name FROM customers
UNION
SELECT name FROM suppliers
ORDER BY name;
choices: Only to the suppliers query, the one it follows
Nowhere; ORDER BY is an error after a UNION
To each SELECT separately, before they are merged
To the combined result of the whole UNION
questions.why: A trailing ORDER BY sorts the final result of the set operation. To sort or limit one branch on its own you need parentheses or a subquery. UNION also removes duplicates, which any per-branch ordering would not survive anyway.
questions.asked: It checks you know set operations produce one result that is then ordered.

questions.q: What does `SELECT customer_id FROM orders INTERSECT SELECT id FROM vip_customers` return?
choices: Customer ids found in both queries, with duplicates removed
Customer ids found in either query, with duplicates removed
Customer ids found in orders but not in vip_customers
Every pairing of order rows with VIP rows that share an id
questions.why: INTERSECT keeps distinct rows present in both results, like an inner semi-join on all columns. Either-side is UNION, orders-but-not-VIP is EXCEPT, and pairings are a join, which would also repeat an id per order.
questions.asked: Set operators are compact answers to 'in both lists' questions that people otherwise write as awkward joins.

questions.q: `WHERE name LIKE 'ann%'` finds 'Ann Lee' in SQLite and on a default SQL Server install, but not in Postgres. Why?
choices: Postgres needs `%` escaped as `%%` inside a LIKE pattern
Postgres LIKE is case-sensitive; the others are not here
Postgres LIKE matches whole words only, not prefixes
Postgres LIKE requires an index before it matches anything
questions.why: Postgres LIKE compares case-sensitively (use ILIKE or lower()), SQLite's LIKE is case-insensitive for ASCII, and SQL Server follows the column collation, whose default is case-insensitive. Prefix matching with `%` works the same in all three.
questions.asked: Search behaving differently after a database switch is a real migration surprise.

questions.q: In Postgres, how do you stop 'Ann@x.com' and 'ann@x.com' registering as two accounts?
choices: A UNIQUE constraint on email, which ignores case by default
A CHECK constraint that email is equal to lower(email)
A unique index on lower(email), or the citext column type
A trigger that deletes the older row on each new insert
questions.why: Postgres text comparison is case-sensitive, so a plain UNIQUE treats the two as different. A unique expression index on `lower(email)` (queried with `lower(email) = lower($1)`) or a citext column enforces it. A CHECK forcing lower case works only if every writer normalises input.
questions.asked: Case-insensitive uniqueness for emails and usernames is a standard sign-up requirement.

questions.q: Which query returns the five best-selling products by units from `order_lines (product_id, qty)`?
choices: SELECT product_id, MAX(qty) AS units FROM order_lines GROUP BY product_id ORDER BY units DESC LIMIT 5;
SELECT TOP 5 product_id FROM order_lines GROUP BY product_id HAVING MAX(qty) > 0;
SELECT product_id, COUNT(qty) AS units FROM order_lines GROUP BY product_id ORDER BY units LIMIT 5;
SELECT product_id, SUM(qty) AS units FROM order_lines GROUP BY product_id ORDER BY units DESC LIMIT 5;
questions.why: You need total units per product: group, SUM, sort descending, then limit (TOP 5 or FETCH FIRST in SQL Server). The MAX version ranks each product's biggest single line, the COUNT version counts lines ascending, and the HAVING version never sorts.
questions.asked: A 'top N by total' report is the most common aggregation question in interviews.

questions.q: What makes this subquery correlated, and what does that mean?
questions.code:
SELECT c.name,
  (SELECT MAX(o.created_at) FROM orders o
   WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) AS last_order
FROM customers c;
choices: It refers to c.id; it is evaluated for each customer row
It uses MAX; the engine caches one maximum for all rows
It sits in SELECT; it is run once and joined to every row
It has no GROUP BY; the engine rejects it on large tables
questions.why: A correlated subquery references the outer query, so logically it runs per outer row; with an index on `orders (customer_id, created_at)` that is cheap, and optimisers may turn it into a join. It returns NULL for customers without orders, unlike an inner join with GROUP BY.
questions.asked: Correlated subqueries are readable and often fine; interviewers want you to know their cost model.

questions.q: Is `COUNT(1)` faster than `COUNT(*)` in Postgres, SQL Server or MySQL?
choices: Yes, COUNT(*) reads every column of each row
No, both count rows and are planned the same way
No, COUNT(*) is faster because 1 is evaluated per row
Yes, COUNT(1) can use an index but COUNT(*) cannot
questions.why: `COUNT(*)` means 'count rows' and never reads column values; `COUNT(1)` counts a non-NULL constant, so the result and plan are the same (Postgres is marginally faster with `*`). `COUNT(col)` is the one that differs, because it skips NULLs.
questions.asked: It is a myth check: strong candidates move the conversation to COUNT(col) versus COUNT(*).

questions.q: A query was written as `SELECT * FROM orders, customers WHERE orders.total > 100`. Why does it return millions of rows?
choices: The comma syntax is a LEFT JOIN, which keeps unmatched rows
The WHERE clause is applied after LIMIT, so it has no effect
No join condition, so each order pairs with every customer
The comma syntax is a UNION, which stacks both tables' rows
questions.why: Listing tables with commas is an old-style inner join whose condition belongs in WHERE; without `orders.customer_id = customers.id` it becomes a cross join. Explicit `JOIN ... ON` syntax makes a missing condition much harder to miss.
questions.asked: Accidental cross joins are a classic outage-inducing mistake and a reason teams mandate explicit JOIN syntax.

questions.q: Adding `JOIN prices p ON p.product_id = o.product_id` to an orders report doubled its row count and revenue. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The join became a cross join because product_id is not a key
The optimiser duplicated rows while using a hash join strategy
The JOIN defaulted to a FULL OUTER JOIN and added unmatched rows
prices has several rows per product, such as one per date range
questions.why: A join returns one row per matching pair, so a product with two price rows doubles each order. Join on the full key (product plus the effective date range) or pick one row per product first. Join algorithms never change results, and JOIN means INNER JOIN.
questions.asked: Row multiplication after a join is the most common reporting bug, and diagnosing it quickly is a mid-level skill.

questions.q: `purchases (customer_id, product_id)` may repeat pairs. Which query finds customers who bought both product 1 and product 2?
choices: SELECT customer_id FROM purchases WHERE product_id IN (1, 2) GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT product_id) = 2;
SELECT customer_id FROM purchases WHERE product_id = 1 AND product_id = 2 GROUP BY customer_id;
SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM purchases WHERE product_id IN (1, 2) ORDER BY customer_id;
SELECT customer_id FROM purchases WHERE product_id IN (1, 2) GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) = 2;
questions.why: Filter to the two products, group per customer and require two distinct products. A single row cannot have two product ids, IN alone finds either product, and COUNT(*) = 2 is fooled by someone who bought product 1 twice.
questions.asked: 'Has all of these' questions show whether you can move from row filters to group-level conditions.

questions.q: In Postgres, SQL Server or SQLite, a `middle_name` column holds `''` for some rows and NULL for others. What does `WHERE middle_name IS NULL` return?
choices: Every such row, since an empty string is stored as NULL
Only the NULL rows; an empty string is a real value
Only the '' rows, since NULL cannot be tested this way
Neither kind, because IS NULL needs a NOT NULL column
questions.why: In these engines '' is a known, empty value and NULL is unknown or absent, so they need separate handling (Oracle is the exception that treats '' as NULL). Decide on one representation, often NULL plus a CHECK against '', so queries stay simple.
questions.asked: Mixed '' and NULL values cause filters that silently miss rows.

questions.q: In Postgres, why is `SELECT count(*) FROM events` on a 500-million-row table slow even though `id` is the primary key?
choices: Primary key indexes are not used for aggregates in Postgres
count(*) reads every column, unlike count(id), which uses the key
MVCC gives no single row count, so rows must be visited
count(*) takes an exclusive lock and waits for all writers first
questions.why: Different transactions can see different row sets, so Postgres cannot keep a single stored count and must scan the table or an index (with visibility checks). For a dashboard, `reltuples` from pg_class gives a fast estimate, or maintain a counter table. count(*) takes no blocking lock.
questions.asked: Paginated UIs showing exact totals on huge tables are a common performance trap.

questions.q: Tasks must be listed urgent first, then open, then everything else, with id as a tiebreaker. What is the idiomatic ORDER BY?
choices: ORDER BY status IN ('urgent', 'open') DESC, status, id
ORDER BY status = 'urgent' DESC, status = 'open', id
ORDER BY status DESC, id
ORDER BY CASE status WHEN 'urgent' THEN 0 WHEN 'open' THEN 1 ELSE 2 END, id
questions.why: A CASE expression maps each status to a sort rank, which works in every engine. Alphabetical DESC matches only by coincidence and breaks once a status like 'review' exists; the IN version sorts open before urgent, and `status = 'open'` ascending puts open rows last.
questions.asked: Custom sort orders come up in every task or ticket UI.

questions.q: A customer has many orders; each order belongs to one customer. Where does the foreign key go?
choices: orders.customer_id, pointing at the owning customer
customers.order_id, pointing at the customer's latest order
A customer_orders junction table holding both ids
On both tables, each pointing at the other one
questions.why: In one-to-many the 'many' side holds the reference, because each order has exactly one customer, while a customer can have any number of orders. A junction table is for many-to-many, and mutual FKs create a circular dependency that complicates inserts.
questions.asked: It is the first modelling question in most interviews and anchors everything after it.

questions.q: Each user has at most one profile row with extra settings. What is the usual way to enforce one-to-one?
choices: users.profile_id with a plain index, so profile lookups are quick
user_profiles.user_id as a foreign key that is also UNIQUE
A user_profile_links junction table holding two foreign keys
A CHECK constraint on users that counts matching profile rows
questions.why: A foreign key alone allows many profiles per user; making user_id unique (often the profile's primary key too) caps it at one. An index on the other side does not enforce anything, and CHECK constraints cannot count rows in another table.
questions.asked: One-to-one looks trivial, but most candidates forget the uniqueness half.

questions.q: Why store phone numbers in a text column rather than an integer column?
choices: Integer columns cannot hold more than about seven digits
Text columns are faster to index and compare than integers
Integers drop leading zeros and '+', and no maths is done on them
Integer columns cannot be given a UNIQUE constraint in most engines
questions.why: A phone number is an identifier made of digits, not a quantity: '07700' becomes 7700 and '+44' cannot be stored. The same reasoning applies to postcodes and account numbers. Integers index well and allow UNIQUE; bigint holds 19 digits.
questions.asked: Type choice questions reveal whether you think about what data means, not just what it looks like.

questions.q: A user may review each product at most once. What enforces that in the database?
choices: A NOT NULL constraint on both user_id and product_id columns
A UNIQUE constraint on the user_id column of the reviews table
A foreign key from reviews.user_id to the users.id column
A UNIQUE constraint on (user_id, product_id) in reviews
questions.why: A composite unique constraint allows each pair once, so a user can review many products and a product can have many reviewers. Unique on user_id alone limits each user to one review in total; foreign keys and NOT NULL only ensure the ids exist.
questions.asked: Business rules like 'once per' are best enforced by the database, and this is the simplest example.

questions.q: Which type do you normally use for a true/false flag in SQL Server?
choices: bit, which stores 0, 1 or NULL
boolean, the same as Postgres
tinyint with a CHECK for 0 or 1
char(1) holding 'Y' or 'N'
questions.why: SQL Server has no boolean column type; `bit` is the idiomatic flag, and EF Core maps C# bool to it. Postgres has a real `boolean`. The tinyint and 'Y'/'N' patterns work but add constraints and conversions for no gain.
questions.asked: Knowing each engine's basic types avoids awkward schema designs when switching stacks.

questions.q: A `posts` table stores tags as `'sql,react,css'` in one column. What is the main problem?
choices: Text columns cannot store commas unless each one is escaped
It breaks 1NF: tags cannot be indexed, joined or constrained
It takes far more storage than a separate tags table would
It breaks 2NF, because the table's primary key is composite
questions.why: Multiple values in one column break 1NF: finding posts tagged 'sql' needs string matching (slow and error-prone), renaming a tag means rewriting strings, and nothing stops misspelt tags. A post_tags junction table fixes all three. Commas are ordinary characters.
questions.asked: Spotting a repeated group in one column is the most practical normalisation skill.

questions.q: Students enrol in many courses and each enrolment has a grade. Where should `grade` live?
choices: On students, as one column per course taken
On courses, as the average of all students' grades
On the enrolments junction table, beside both ids
In a JSON column on students keyed by course id
questions.why: The grade is a fact about the pair (this student in this course), so it belongs on the junction row. Junction tables often carry such attributes: joined_at, role, quantity. Per-course columns and JSON maps lose constraints and indexability.
questions.asked: It checks whether you see a junction table as a real entity rather than plumbing.

questions.q: Why use a `countries` lookup table with a foreign key instead of letting users type a free-text country?
choices: Free-text columns cannot be indexed or sorted reliably in SQL
Foreign keys are required on every column that users can edit
Lookup tables speed up every query by avoiding string compares
It keeps values consistent: no 'UK' beside 'United Kingdom'
questions.why: A foreign key restricts values to known rows, so grouping and filtering work reliably and renames happen in one place. Free text can be indexed, and lookups add a join rather than making everything faster; the benefit is data quality.
questions.asked: Data quality is a design choice, and interviewers like candidates who push rules into the schema.

questions.q: Why declare columns NOT NULL wherever the value is always required?
choices: It rejects missing data at write time and simplifies every query
NOT NULL columns take noticeably less disk space than nullable ones
Nullable columns cannot be included in any index on the table
NOT NULL forces you to give the column a default value as well
questions.why: The constraint rejects bad writes from any code path, and readers no longer need IS NULL handling or COALESCE for impossible cases. Storage savings are minor, nullable columns can be indexed, and NOT NULL does not require a default.
questions.asked: Defaulting to nullable everywhere is a common junior habit that interviewers probe.

questions.q: `products` has a surrogate `id` primary key. Why add a UNIQUE constraint on `sku` as well?
choices: The primary key index cannot be used for lookups by sku
The id alone lets the same real product be inserted twice
A table must have at least two unique columns to be valid
UNIQUE on sku makes id generation faster for new rows
questions.why: A surrogate id is always unique, so it never detects duplicates of the real-world thing; the natural key (sku, email, ISBN) still needs its own unique constraint. That constraint also gives you an index for lookups by sku.
questions.asked: Surrogate keys without natural-key constraints are a common source of duplicate data.

questions.q: `orders.coupon_id` is a nullable foreign key. What does a NULL there mean?
choices: The coupon row was deleted and the FK was switched off
The coupon exists but has not been loaded by the ORM
The order has no coupon; the relationship is optional
The foreign key check is skipped until the order is paid
questions.why: Foreign keys only check non-NULL values, so a nullable FK models an optional relationship (zero or one coupon), while NOT NULL makes it mandatory. Deleting a referenced coupon is blocked or handled by the ON DELETE rule, not by nulls appearing on their own.
questions.asked: Optional versus required relationships are the first thing to decide when adding a foreign key.

questions.q: `orders` stores `customer_id` and also `customer_city`, copied from `customers`. What problem does this create?
choices: A foreign key cannot exist while a copy of the column is present
The copy makes customer_id a composite primary key
Queries on orders become slower because rows are wider
A customer who moves leaves old orders and customers disagreeing
questions.why: customer_city depends on the customer, not the order: a transitive dependency that breaks third normal form, so an update in one place leaves stale copies (an update anomaly). The exception is when you deliberately want the city at the time of the order, which is a different fact.
questions.asked: Explaining normal forms through anomalies, not definitions, is what interviewers are really after.

questions.q: `order_lines` stores `unit_price` even though `products.price` exists. Is that a normalisation mistake?
choices: No; it records the price charged at the time, a different fact
Yes; the line should always join to products for its current price
Yes; it is acceptable only if a trigger keeps the two in sync
No; duplicating any column is always fine for read performance
questions.why: The product's price changes over time, but the invoice must not, so the line's price is its own historical fact. Syncing it with a trigger would rewrite past invoices. The same applies to shipping addresses and tax rates on orders.
questions.asked: Distinguishing a snapshot from a duplicate shows real-world modelling judgement.

questions.q: In Postgres, what is the main downside of a native `CREATE TYPE status AS ENUM (...)` compared with a lookup table or a CHECK constraint?
choices: Enum columns cannot be indexed or used in a WHERE clause at all
Values can be added, but removing one means rebuilding the type
Each enum value takes more storage than the equivalent text value
Enum types are visible only to the database role that created them
questions.why: `ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE` and `RENAME VALUE` work, but dropping a value means creating a new type and migrating columns. A lookup table can also carry labels and ordering and be changed by data, not DDL. Enums index fine and are compact (4 bytes).
questions.asked: Status columns exist in every app, and the enum-versus-table choice has long-term migration cost.

questions.q: `orders.total` is stored as well as being derivable from `order_lines`. What must the code do to keep it trustworthy?
choices: Recompute it nightly with a batch job, since drift is expected
Store it as a float so rounding differences cannot build up
Update it in the same transaction as any line change
Mark the column UNIQUE so duplicate totals are rejected
questions.why: A stored aggregate is deliberate denormalisation: faster reads, but every write path must update it atomically with the lines, or readers see a total that disagrees with them. A nightly job leaves hours of wrong data; floats make money worse, not better.
questions.asked: Denormalising is fine when you name the consistency cost, which is what interviewers want to hear.

questions.q: In SQL Server 2022, why prefer `datetime2` (or `datetimeoffset`) over `datetime` for new columns?
choices: datetime cannot be indexed or used as part of a clustered key
datetime2 stores an IANA time zone name alongside each value
datetime always stores server local time, even when sent UTC
datetime rounds to about 3 ms; datetime2 is precise to 100 ns
questions.why: Legacy datetime has 1/300-second precision and a 1753 lower bound, so .NET DateTime values get rounded and equality checks fail. datetime2 matches .NET precision; datetimeoffset adds the UTC offset (not a zone name). datetime stores whatever value you send.
questions.asked: Rounding bugs between .NET and datetime are common in older schemas.

questions.q: In Postgres, why use the `uuid` type rather than `varchar(36)` for UUID keys?
choices: uuid takes 16 bytes and rejects malformed values; text does not
varchar columns cannot hold hyphens when used as a primary key
uuid values are generated faster when the column type is uuid
varchar keys cannot be the target of foreign keys in Postgres
questions.why: The native type stores the 128 bits in 16 bytes, rejects malformed input and compares faster, which matters in every index and foreign key that repeats it. Generation speed is unrelated to storage type, and text keys can be referenced normally.
questions.asked: Key types multiply through indexes and joins, so small choices matter at scale.

questions.q: In SQL Server 2016+, what does a system-versioned temporal table give you?
choices: Automatic deletion of rows older than a configured retention period
A history table of old row versions, queryable AS OF a past time
A copy of the table on a read replica, refreshed once every minute
Row-level locks that are released automatically after a set time
questions.why: The engine moves each old row version into a history table with validity periods on every UPDATE and DELETE, so 'what did this row look like last Tuesday?' is a query, not custom audit code. Retention can be configured, but history is the point.
questions.asked: Audit history is a common requirement, and built-in features beat hand-written triggers.

questions.q: A multi-tenant SaaS keeps every tenant in shared tables with a `tenant_id` column. What is the biggest risk, and a database-level guard?
choices: Tables grow too large; guard with one database per tenant
Ids collide between tenants; guard with a composite primary key
A query missing the filter leaks data; use row-level security
Tenants lock each other's rows; guard with SERIALIZABLE isolation
questions.why: One forgotten `WHERE tenant_id = ...` exposes other customers' data. Postgres row-level security (or SQL Server security policies) applies the filter to every query based on a session setting, and ORMs add global query filters. Surrogate ids do not collide.
questions.asked: Tenant isolation is a top concern in B2B apps, and naming a defence beyond 'be careful' is expected.

questions.q: You need an order's current status and its full status history. What is a common, robust design?
choices: Just a status column on orders, overwritten on each change
One nullable timestamp column per status, like paid_at, shipped_at
Just a JSON array of past statuses appended to on the order row
A status_events table, plus a current status updated alongside
questions.why: An append-only events table keeps who changed what and when, while a denormalised current status keeps list queries simple; updating both in one transaction keeps them consistent. Overwriting loses history, a JSON array loses constraints, and per-status columns cannot record a status twice.
questions.asked: Workflow history is in every order, ticket and approval system.

questions.q: Two requests add a comment at the same moment, and each runs this. Why is the count sometimes one too low?
choices: Each request reads the same n, so both write n + 1
The UPDATE takes a table lock and drops the second write
The parameter @n is cached by the plan from the first call
The second UPDATE fails silently on a unique constraint
questions.why: Read-then-write in the app is a lost update: both read 5 and both write 6. `SET comment_count = comment_count + 1` makes the database do the increment atomically under the row lock, so both land. Plan caching affects plans, not parameter values.
questions.asked: Counters are the simplest lost-update example, and atomic updates are the simplest fix.

questions.q: Where should user-uploaded images usually be stored in a typical web app?
choices: In a varbinary or bytea column, so backups always include them
In object storage such as S3, with the object key in the database
On the web server's local disk, with the file path in the database
Base64-encoded in a text column, so JSON APIs can return them as-is
questions.why: Object storage is cheap, scales separately and serves files via a CDN, while the database keeps small metadata rows. Large blobs in the database bloat backups and memory, local disk vanishes with a container or is not shared across instances, and Base64 adds a third in size.
questions.asked: File storage design comes up in every CRUD app with uploads.

questions.q: An API exposes orders at `/orders/1041`, using the sequential primary key. Why do many teams expose a separate random public id?
choices: Sequential ids are not permitted in URLs under RFC 9110 rules
Primary keys change when rows are updated, breaking old links
Sequential ids reveal volume and invite guessing other records
Random ids make database joins faster than integer ids can be
questions.why: Consecutive numbers leak business volume and make it trivial to try 1042, 1043: if an authorisation check is missed, that becomes an IDOR breach. A random public id (UUID or slug) reduces exposure, though authorisation checks are still the real fix. Primary keys do not change.
questions.asked: Id design links data modelling to security, which interviewers like to probe together.

questions.q: Why do many teams use `bigint` rather than `int` for primary keys on tables that grow fast?
choices: bigint keys are compared faster than int keys by the CPU
bigint is the only key type that foreign keys can reference
int keys cannot be generated by an identity column or sequence
int tops out near 2.1 billion, and changing it later is painful
questions.why: A signed int identity runs out at 2,147,483,647, and gaps from rollbacks use values up faster; migrating a primary key and every foreign key to bigint on a live table is a major operation. The extra 4 bytes per row are usually a cheap insurance premium.
questions.asked: Running out of int ids is a real outage story, and planning for growth is a mid-level trait.

questions.q: Each order line must reference a product from the same tenant. In Postgres or SQL Server, how can the schema enforce that?
choices: A composite FK (tenant_id, product_id) to products (tenant_id, id)
A CHECK constraint comparing the two tables' tenant_id values
Two separate foreign keys, one on tenant_id and one on product_id
A unique index on order_lines covering (tenant_id, product_id)
questions.why: Carrying tenant_id in the foreign key forces the referenced product to have the same tenant. CHECK constraints cannot look at other tables, two separate FKs check each value independently, and a unique index limits duplicates instead of checking ownership.
questions.asked: Cross-tenant references are a subtle data leak that composite keys prevent structurally.

questions.q: Room bookings must never overlap for the same room. In Postgres, what enforces this in the schema?
choices: A UNIQUE constraint across (room_id, starts_at, ends_at) columns
EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&)
A CHECK constraint comparing ends_at with other rows' starts_at
A self-referencing foreign key from bookings.room_id to bookings
questions.why: An exclusion constraint rejects a row if any existing row matches on every listed operator: same room and overlapping range (`&&` on a tstzrange; the btree_gist extension is needed for `=` on the id). UNIQUE only blocks identical times, and CHECK cannot see other rows. In SQL Server you would need a transaction with locking or a trigger.
questions.asked: Double bookings are a classic race, and a database-level answer shows depth.

questions.q: In Postgres, what is the difference between `ON DELETE RESTRICT` and the default `ON DELETE NO ACTION`?
choices: RESTRICT deletes the child rows; NO ACTION leaves them orphaned
RESTRICT applies only to updates; NO ACTION only to deletes
RESTRICT checks at once; NO ACTION at statement end, deferrably
They differ only in the wording of the error message raised
questions.why: Both reject deleting a referenced parent, but NO ACTION runs its check at the end of the statement (or at commit if the constraint is DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED), so a statement that also fixes the children can succeed. RESTRICT checks immediately. SQL Server only offers NO ACTION.
questions.asked: It separates people who have read the constraint docs from those who only know CASCADE.

questions.q: Playlist items have `UNIQUE (playlist_id, position)`. Why does `UPDATE items SET position = position + 1 WHERE playlist_id = 7` fail in Postgres, and what is one fix?
choices: UPDATE cannot touch a column in a unique constraint; drop and re-add it
The WHERE matches too many rows at once; update positions one by one
Arithmetic on key columns is not allowed; compute positions in the app
The check runs per row mid-update and collides; make it DEFERRABLE
questions.why: Postgres checks a non-deferrable unique constraint as each row is updated, so moving 1 to 2 collides with the existing 2 depending on row order. Declaring it `DEFERRABLE` (checked at statement end or commit) fixes it; gapped or fractional positions avoid renumbering entirely.
questions.asked: Reordering lists is a common feature that runs straight into this constraint behaviour.

questions.q: `comments` has `commentable_type` ('post' or 'photo') and `commentable_id`. What does this polymorphic design give up?
choices: commentable_id cannot have a real foreign key to either table
Comments can no longer be sorted reliably by their creation time
Each comment row can only be loaded by one ORM entity at a time
Posts and photos can no longer use integer primary key columns
questions.why: A foreign key must reference one table, so the database cannot stop comments pointing at deleted or non-existent parents, and joins need the type column. Alternatives are one nullable FK per parent with a CHECK that exactly one is set, or separate post_comments and photo_comments tables.
questions.asked: Polymorphic associations are common in Rails-style apps, and seniors can name the trade-off and alternatives.

questions.q: A design proposes `attributes (entity_id, name, value text)` so any product can have any field. What is the main problem with this entity-attribute-value model?
choices: It cannot store more than one attribute value for each entity
Values lose types and constraints; filters need many self-joins
It forces every product to carry exactly the same attribute set
It needs a new table to be created for every attribute name added
questions.why: Everything becomes text, so nothing checks that weight is a number or that required fields exist, and filtering on three attributes means three joins or pivots. A JSON column with validation, or real columns for common fields, is usually the better compromise.
questions.asked: EAV keeps being reinvented; recognising it and offering alternatives is a senior-leaning signal.

questions.q: Categories are stored with `parent_id` (an adjacency list). The UI constantly needs 'all descendants of X' on a deep tree. What alternative model makes that a simple indexed query?
choices: A trigger copying each category's child ids into a text column
A self-join repeated once per level of the deepest branch
A materialised path like '/1/4/9/', or a closure table
A table per level, such as level1_categories, level2_categories
questions.why: A path column turns 'descendants of 4' into a prefix match (`LIKE '/1/4/%'`), and a closure table into a plain join, each served by an index. The adjacency list is simplest for writes and fine with recursive CTEs; the alternatives trade write complexity for fast reads. Postgres's ltree type implements the path idea.
questions.asked: Trees appear in categories, comments and org charts, and knowing more than parent_id shows range.

questions.q: A booking app stores a dentist appointment for 9:00 next March in London as a UTC timestamp. What can go wrong?
choices: UTC cannot represent a time that is more than a year in the future
Nothing can go wrong; UTC is always correct for every timestamp
UTC timestamps lose their minutes when converted to London time
If DST rules change before then, the instant no longer means 9:00
questions.why: For past events UTC is right, but a future local appointment is really 'wall-clock 9:00 in Europe/London'; if the government changes DST rules, the precomputed UTC instant becomes 8:00 or 10:00. Store the local time plus the IANA zone id and compute the instant when needed.
questions.asked: It is a known exception to 'always store UTC', and mentioning it signals real scheduling experience.

questions.q: An ORM maps `Payment` with subclasses `CardPayment` and `BankPayment`. What is the trade-off of one table with a discriminator column (table-per-hierarchy) versus a table per subclass?
choices: One table avoids joins but forces subclass columns to be nullable
One table needs joins on every read; per-subclass tables never do
One table cannot hold rows for more than two subclasses at a time
Per-subclass tables cannot have foreign keys to the base table
questions.why: Table-per-hierarchy (EF Core's default) keeps reads join-free, but card-only columns must allow NULL for bank rows, so NOT NULL rules move to CHECK constraints or code. Table-per-type keeps columns strict at the cost of joins on every query; the subclass tables reference the base table by foreign key.
questions.asked: Inheritance mapping comes up once domain models get richer, and the NULL trade-off is the key insight.

questions.q: Which parameter placeholder style does each Node driver use: node-postgres (`pg`), `mysql2` and `mssql` (SQL Server)?
choices: pg: ?; mysql2: $1; mssql: :name
pg: $1; mysql2: ?; mssql: @name
pg: @name; mysql2: $1; mssql: ?
pg: :name; mysql2: @name; mssql: $1
questions.why: node-postgres uses Postgres's numbered `$1, $2` placeholders, mysql2 uses positional `?`, and mssql binds named `@name` inputs via `.input()`. Mixing them up produces syntax errors, which is why some teams hide the difference behind a query builder.
questions.asked: Writing a parameterised query from memory in your stack's driver is a basic practical check.

questions.q: What is the difference between a migration and a seed script?
choices: Migrations insert sample rows; seeds change the table structure
Migrations run only in production; seeds run only in development
Migrations change schema in order; seeds load starting data
Migrations are written in SQL; seeds must be written in the ORM
questions.why: Migrations are versioned, ordered schema changes applied once per database; seeds insert reference or sample data and are often rerunnable. Reference data every environment needs (such as countries) is sometimes shipped in a migration instead, but demo users never should be.
questions.asked: Keeping schema and data concerns apart avoids fragile deployments.

questions.q: Nightly database backups have run for a year. What is the only way to know they work?
choices: Check that each night's backup file has a non-zero size
Confirm the backup job's exit code in the scheduler logs
Compare backup file checksums with the previous night's
Restore one regularly on another server and query it
questions.why: Backups fail in ways a job log never shows: missing permissions, excluded databases, corrupt files, or a restore that takes longer than the business can wait. A scheduled test restore proves both the data and the recovery time. Checksums only show the file did not change.
questions.asked: Interviewers like hearing 'an untested backup is not a backup' because it signals production experience.

questions.q: What is a read replica mainly used for?
choices: Serving read queries to take load off the primary
Taking writes when the primary database is too busy
Keeping deleted rows so they can be restored later
Running migrations before they reach the primary
questions.why: A replica streams changes from the primary and accepts reads only, so reports and heavy list queries can move there. It lags slightly behind the primary, which matters for read-after-write flows. It is not a backup: a bad DELETE replicates too.
questions.asked: Scaling reads is the first database-scaling step, and interviewers expect you to mention lag.

questions.q: An app runs BEGIN, two INSERTs, then the network drops before COMMIT is sent. What happens to the two rows in Postgres or SQL Server?
choices: They stay committed, because each INSERT succeeded on its own
They are rolled back when the server notices the dead session
The first stays and the second is rolled back automatically
They stay locked, uncommitted, until an administrator steps in
questions.why: Nothing inside an open transaction is durable until COMMIT succeeds, and when the server detects the lost connection it aborts the transaction and releases its locks. That is atomicity in practice: all or nothing. The app must treat the outcome as unknown and retry idempotently.
questions.asked: Reasoning about failure mid-transaction is what atomicity is for.

questions.q: Which database login should a production web app use?
choices: The server admin (sa or postgres), so every query works
The database owner, so the app can run migrations too
A login with only the data rights the app needs
A separate login per end user of the web application
questions.why: Least privilege limits the blast radius of SQL injection or a leaked connection string: no DROP, no access to other databases, no server settings. Migrations run under a separate, more privileged login in the deployment pipeline. Per-end-user logins break connection pooling.
questions.asked: Least privilege on database accounts is a basic security expectation that many apps ignore.

questions.q: What is the quickest way to spot an N+1 query problem while developing an endpoint?
choices: Measure the response size of the endpoint in the browser
Check CPU usage on the database server while you click around
Look for SELECT * in the ORM's generated SQL statements
Turn on SQL logging and count the queries one request runs
questions.why: N+1 shows up as the same query repeated once per row, which SQL logging (EF Core's `LogTo`, Prisma's query log, or a pg statement log) makes obvious. With small dev data the endpoint may still feel fast and CPU stays low, so timing alone hides it.
questions.asked: Knowing how to see the SQL your ORM runs is a core mid-level habit.

questions.q: `products` has an index on `name`. Can it help `SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY name LIMIT 20`?
choices: Yes, the engine can read the first 20 entries in order
No, indexes only help WHERE clauses and never ORDER BY
No, LIMIT forces the engine to sort every row first
Yes, but only when the table has under 20 rows total
questions.why: A B-tree keeps entries sorted, so the engine can walk the index from the start and stop after 20 rows without sorting the table. Whether it chooses to depends on costs, but ORDER BY with LIMIT is one of the best cases for an index.
questions.asked: Indexes serve sorting as well as filtering, which many juniors do not realise.

questions.q: In a migration tool with `up` and `down` methods, what is `down` for?
choices: Running before `up` to check that the database is reachable
Reverting that migration's change, mostly in local dev
Deleting every row the migration's `up` step has inserted
Downgrading the database engine to its previous version
questions.why: `down` undoes the schema change so you can roll back and iterate locally. In production teams usually roll forward with a new migration, since reversing a destructive change (a dropped column) cannot bring the data back.
questions.asked: It opens the discussion about rolling back versus rolling forward in production.

questions.q: In Postgres, what is `public` in `SELECT * FROM public.users`?
choices: A permission level that lets any role read the table
The name of the database the table is stored in
The default schema, a namespace inside the database
A flag marking the table as replicated to readers
questions.why: Postgres databases contain schemas, and tables live in a schema; `public` is the default one found via search_path. Schemas group tables (for example per module or tenant) and carry permissions. SQL Server's equivalent default is `dbo`.
questions.asked: Qualified names appear in every migration, and knowing schema versus database avoids confusion.

questions.q: Developers want a copy of production data to debug an issue locally. What must happen first?
choices: Nothing, as long as the copy stays on company laptops
Indexes are dropped so the copy uses less disk space
The copy is compressed so it downloads in reasonable time
Personal data is masked or anonymised before it leaves
questions.why: Real names, emails and addresses on laptops are a privacy and GDPR liability. Mask or synthesise personal data (keeping shapes and volumes), or debug against a secured staging copy. Compression and disk space are conveniences, not safeguards.
questions.asked: Handling production data responsibly is part of being trusted with database access.

questions.q: Why should each migration be small and do one logical change?
choices: Small steps are easier to review, deploy and roll forward
Migration tools refuse files with more than one statement
Engines can only lock one table per migration transaction
Large migrations are silently skipped by most ORM tools
questions.why: A focused migration is easy to review, fails in an obvious place, and fits expand-and-contract deployments where each step must be compatible with running code. Tools happily run multi-statement migrations; the size is about safety, not a limit.
questions.asked: Migration hygiene is a proxy for how carefully someone ships schema changes.

questions.q: With node-postgres, why does this sometimes run the INSERTs outside the transaction?
choices: pool.query cannot run BEGIN; transactions need pool.transaction()
Each pool.query may use a different connection from the pool
node-postgres wraps each query in its own implicit SAVEPOINT
The awaits let other requests interleave inside the same BEGIN
questions.why: A transaction belongs to one connection, but `pool.query` borrows any free client for each call, so BEGIN and the INSERTs can land on different sessions. Use `const client = await pool.connect()`, run everything on that client, and `client.release()` in a finally block.
questions.asked: It is the most common transaction bug in Node apps and a favourite code-review question.

questions.q: With node-postgres defaults, `SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM users` gives `rows[0].n`. What type is it in JavaScript?
choices: number, because COUNT always returns a small integer
bigint, because pg maps int8 to the JavaScript BigInt type
string, since COUNT returns bigint, which pg leaves unparsed
number, unless the table holds more than 2^31 rows
questions.why: Postgres COUNT returns bigint (int8), and node-postgres returns int8 as a string by default because it can exceed Number's safe range. `n === 5` then fails silently. Cast in SQL (`COUNT(*)::int`) or register a type parser.
questions.asked: String counts cause subtle comparison and JSON bugs in Node APIs.

questions.q: Your app runs pending migrations at startup, and you deploy four instances at once. What can go wrong?
choices: Nothing, because migration tools always run each file once
Only the first instance to start will be able to connect at all
The instances run migrations in alphabetical order, not by version
Several instances may apply the same migration at the same time
questions.why: Unless the tool takes a lock (some do, via an advisory lock or lock table), parallel startups race and fail or double-apply. Running migrations as a separate deployment step before rollout avoids the race and keeps app logins unprivileged.
questions.asked: Scaling out exposes startup-time side effects, and migrations are the classic one.

questions.q: A user edits their profile and the page reloads showing the old name. Reads go to a replica. What is the likely cause and a fix?
choices: Replication lag; read from the primary right after writes
The write failed; retry it until the replica shows the change
Browser caching; add a random query string to every request
The ORM cached the entity; restart the app to clear it
questions.why: Asynchronous replicas trail the primary by milliseconds to seconds, so a read right after a write can miss it. Routing a user's reads to the primary for a short time after they write (read-your-writes) or returning the updated row from the write fixes it.
questions.asked: Replicas trade consistency for scale, and interviewers want to see you handle the lag.

questions.q: What is the main trade-off of putting business logic in stored procedures rather than in application code?
choices: Procedures cannot use transactions, so logic is less safe
Fewer round trips, but harder to test, version and deploy
Procedures are always slower because their plans are not cached
Procedures cannot accept parameters, so they invite injection
questions.why: Procedures run close to the data and can cut chatty round trips, but logic in the database is harder to unit test, review and deploy alongside the app, and ties you to one engine. They support transactions and parameters, and their plans are cached.
questions.asked: Teams differ strongly on this; a balanced answer beats dogma.

questions.q: Under load, a Node API starts hanging on every database call, although the database is idle. What is the most likely bug?
choices: The pool size is too large, so the database rejects connections
client.query ignores params, so every query is re-planned
A throwing query skips release(), so clients leak away
pool.connect opens a fresh TCP connection on every call
questions.why: When `client.query` throws, `release()` never runs, so each failure leaks a client; once the pool is empty, callers wait forever. Put `release()` in a finally block, or use `pool.query` for single statements, which releases for you.
questions.asked: Pool exhaustion from leaked connections is a classic production incident.

questions.q: An insert violates a unique constraint. Which error codes identify that, so the API can return 409 Conflict?
choices: Postgres SQLSTATE 40001; SQL Server error 1205
Postgres SQLSTATE 42P01; SQL Server error 208
Postgres SQLSTATE 23503; SQL Server error 547
Postgres SQLSTATE 23505; SQL Server 2627 or 2601
questions.why: 23505 is unique_violation in Postgres; SQL Server raises 2627 for a unique constraint and 2601 for a unique index. 40001 and 1205 are serialisation failure and deadlock, 23503 and 547 are foreign key violations, and 42P01 and 208 mean the table does not exist.
questions.asked: Mapping database errors to HTTP statuses is everyday API work.

questions.q: A data layer retries failed transactions automatically. Which failure should it NOT retry?
choices: A unique constraint violation (23505)
A serialisation failure (SQLSTATE 40001)
A deadlock victim error (40P01 or 1205)
A dropped connection before any statement ran
questions.why: Deadlocks, serialisation failures and connection drops are transient: running the same transaction again can succeed. A unique violation is a deterministic outcome of the data and will fail identically, so it should become a 409 or be handled as a business case.
questions.asked: Retrying the wrong errors hides bugs and multiplies load, so interviewers probe the distinction.

questions.q: A migration dropped a column and was deployed. A day later you find a bug in it. What do teams usually do in production?
choices: Run the migration's down step, which restores the column and its data
Write a new forward migration that fixes the problem
Edit the applied migration file and redeploy it in place
Restore last night's backup over the live database
questions.why: Applied migrations are history: editing them desynchronises environments, and a down step recreates the column empty because the data is gone. A new migration (plus a targeted data restore if needed) rolls forward safely. Restoring a whole backup discards a day of other writes.
questions.asked: Roll-forward thinking is what separates production migration experience from tutorial experience.

questions.q: You must delete 50 million old rows from a busy `events` table. Why delete in batches of, say, 10,000?
choices: DELETE cannot affect more than 65,535 rows in one statement
Batches make the rows recoverable if you need them back later
One huge DELETE holds locks and bloats the log for a long time
Batches let the engine skip writing the deleted rows to the log
questions.why: A single statement runs as one transaction: it holds its locks (SQL Server may escalate to a table lock), grows the transaction log or WAL, and lags replicas until it commits. Small batches commit often and let other work interleave. Partitioning, where available, turns this into a partition drop.
questions.asked: Data retention jobs are common, and doing them without an outage is a practical skill.

questions.q: In SQL Server with the default collation, a UNIQUE constraint on `Username` rejects 'ann' because 'Ann' exists. Why?
choices: UNIQUE constraints always lower-case values before checking
The unique index uses a hash that ignores letter case
SQL Server stores varchar values in upper case internally
The default collation is case-insensitive, so they match
questions.why: Default SQL Server collations such as SQL_Latin1_General_CP1_CI_AS are case-insensitive (CI), so comparisons, sorting and uniqueness treat the two as equal. Postgres behaves the opposite way by default. A case-sensitive collation (CS) on the column changes it.
questions.asked: Collation differences explain many 'works on my database' bugs between engines.

questions.q: A customer is soft-deleted (`deleted_at` set). Their orders have `ON DELETE CASCADE` to customers. What happens to the orders?
choices: Nothing; no DELETE ran, so the cascade never fires
They are deleted, because the cascade fires on deleted_at
They get deleted_at set too, copied by the foreign key
The update fails, because the cascade forbids the change
questions.why: Cascades react to real DELETEs (and key updates), not to setting a column. With soft delete, child rows need explicit handling in code or a trigger, and every query must decide whether to show orders of deleted customers.
questions.asked: Soft delete interacts badly with relational features, and this is the most concrete example.

questions.q: In Postgres, how can you stop a runaway report query from running for an hour and hogging the database?
choices: Set max_connections lower for the reporting role
Set statement_timeout for that role or session
Set work_mem to zero so large sorts fail at once
Set the isolation level to READ UNCOMMITTED
questions.why: statement_timeout cancels any statement running longer than the limit, and can be set per role (`ALTER ROLE reports SET statement_timeout = '30s'`), per session or per transaction. Connection limits do not end long queries, and Postgres treats READ UNCOMMITTED as READ COMMITTED.
questions.asked: Timeouts are a basic production guardrail, and naming the setting shows hands-on experience.

questions.q: A payment API accepts an `Idempotency-Key` header so client retries do not charge twice. What is the core database piece?
choices: A SERIALIZABLE transaction around every payment request
A trigger that deletes duplicate payments once a night
A table keyed by the idempotency key, with a UNIQUE rule
A read replica that stores the responses for replay
questions.why: Inserting the key (with the stored response) under a unique constraint makes the second attempt fail or find the existing row, even when two retries race. SERIALIZABLE alone does not know two requests are the same, and nightly cleanup is too late.
questions.asked: Idempotent writes are a common API design question, and the unique constraint is the heart of it.

questions.q: From Node, you must insert 5,000 rows into Postgres. What is usually the fastest reasonable approach?
choices: 5,000 pool.query calls fired in parallel with Promise.all
One INSERT per row inside a loop with await on each
5,000 separate INSERTs, each in its own transaction
One INSERT with many VALUES rows, or unnest of arrays
questions.why: A multi-row INSERT (batched to stay under the 65,535 parameter limit) or `INSERT ... SELECT * FROM unnest($1::int[], $2::text[])` sends the data in a few round trips and one transaction; COPY is faster still for big loads. Parallel single inserts just exhaust the pool.
questions.asked: Bulk loading is a common task, and round trips dominate its cost.

questions.q: A middleware opens a transaction at the start of every HTTP request and commits at the end. What is the main downside?
choices: Locks and a connection are held for the whole request
Transactions cannot span more than one SQL statement
Reads made inside a transaction can no longer use any index
Each request is forced to run at SERIALIZABLE isolation
questions.why: Every lock taken early lives until the response is built, including time spent calling other services or rendering, which increases blocking and pool usage. Scope transactions to the unit of work that needs atomicity. The isolation level stays at the default.
questions.asked: Transaction scope is an architecture decision, and interviewers want it to be deliberate.

questions.q: A serverless API (one Lambda or Azure Function instance per concurrent request) exhausts Postgres connections under load. What is the usual fix?
choices: Raise max_connections to 10,000 on the database server
Put a pooler such as PgBouncer or RDS Proxy in front
Open a new connection per query and close it straight after
Switch every query to READ UNCOMMITTED to cut lock use
questions.why: Each function instance has its own small pool, so hundreds of instances open hundreds of connections, and each Postgres connection is a process costing memory. A pooler multiplexes many client connections onto a few server ones. Raising max_connections hurts performance; per-query connects add latency.
questions.asked: Serverless plus relational databases is a common architecture trap.

questions.q: Behind PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode, which app behaviour can break?
choices: Plain parameterised SELECTs sent one at a time by the driver
Transactions that contain more than one INSERT statement
Session state such as SET, advisory locks or LISTEN
Queries that read from more than one table using a JOIN
questions.why: In transaction mode each transaction may run on a different server connection, so anything tied to a session (SET without LOCAL, session advisory locks, LISTEN, temp tables, and named prepared statements on PgBouncer before 1.21) can vanish or leak to another client. Ordinary queries and transactions are fine.
questions.asked: It explains strange bugs that appear only in production after a pooler is added.

questions.q: node-postgres returns a `numeric(12,2)` total as the string '19.99'. Why is `parseFloat` for money a poor default?
choices: parseFloat throws on strings that contain a decimal point
The string is already in cents, so parsing doubles the value
parseFloat rounds the value to the nearest whole number
Floats cannot represent most decimals exactly, so sums drift
questions.why: Binary floats approximate values like 0.1, so `0.1 + 0.2` is 0.30000000000000004 and totals can be off by a cent. The driver returns strings precisely to avoid that; keep them as strings, use integer cents, or a decimal library, and do sums in SQL.
questions.asked: Money precision across the database-to-JS boundary is a real bug class in Node APIs.

questions.q: In Postgres, why does updating a non-indexed column (`last_seen_at`) often cost less than updating an indexed one?
choices: It can be a HOT update, skipping every index when none change
Updates to non-indexed columns are written only to memory
Non-indexed columns are stored in a separate, smaller file
Postgres batches non-indexed updates until the next VACUUM
questions.why: Postgres writes a new row version on every update; if no indexed column changes and the page has room, it makes a heap-only tuple and skips every index. Changing an indexed column forces new entries in all indexes. That is one more reason not to index frequently updated columns.
questions.asked: Write amplification from indexes is an advanced performance topic that seniors can explain.

questions.q: An API uses a `version` column for optimistic concurrency. How is it typically exposed over HTTP?
choices: As a cookie the server sets after each successful GET
As an ETag on GET, echoed in If-Match, with 412 on mismatch
As a query-string parameter the server increments on each request
As a response header the client may ignore on updates
questions.why: The ETag carries the version; the client echoes it in `If-Match`, the server runs `UPDATE ... WHERE id = @id AND version = @v`, and zero affected rows means someone else changed it, so 412 Precondition Failed. That turns a database check into standard HTTP semantics.
questions.asked: Connecting the data layer to HTTP semantics is a sign of end-to-end thinking.

questions.q: A service saves an order and then publishes an `OrderPlaced` message to a broker. If it crashes between the two, the message is lost. What pattern fixes this?
choices: Publish first, then save the order if publishing succeeded
Wrap the INSERT and the publish call in one SERIALIZABLE transaction
Write it to an outbox table in the same transaction
Retry the publish call in a loop until the broker acknowledges
questions.why: The transactional outbox makes the order and the message one atomic database write; a relay then publishes outbox rows and marks them sent, at least once. Publishing first can announce orders that never saved, a broker is not part of the database transaction, and retries do nothing if the process died.
questions.asked: Dual writes are a classic distributed-systems trap, even in simple CRUD services.

questions.q: A migration backfills a new column on 80 million rows. What is the usual safe approach in production?
choices: One UPDATE for all rows inside a single long transaction
Run the UPDATE on a read replica and let it copy back
Drop and recreate the table with the column already filled
Small batches by key range, each committed and throttled
questions.why: Batching by primary key ranges (for example 10,000 ids at a time) keeps each transaction short, limits locks and WAL or log bursts, and lets you pause if replica lag grows. A single UPDATE locks many rows for a long time; replicas are read-only.
questions.asked: Backfills are the risky middle step of expand-and-contract migrations.

questions.q: At READ COMMITTED, a report runs `SELECT SUM(amount) FROM debits` then `SELECT SUM(amount) FROM credits`, and they do not balance though transfers always write both. Why, and what fixes it?
choices: Each statement gets a new snapshot; use REPEATABLE READ
SUM skips rows locked by writers; add a NOLOCK hint to both queries
The two queries run on different connections; use a single JOIN
The planner cached an old plan; recompile both queries first
questions.why: READ COMMITTED gives each statement its own snapshot, so a transfer committing between the two SELECTs is half-visible. REPEATABLE READ in Postgres (or SNAPSHOT in SQL Server) gives the whole transaction one snapshot. NOLOCK would add dirty reads, not consistency.
questions.asked: Multi-statement reports are where READ COMMITTED's per-statement snapshot surprises people.

questions.q: In Postgres, `created_at` is `timestamp` (without time zone) and holds UTC values. Why can `WHERE created_at > now() - interval '1 hour'` be wrong?
choices: Interval arithmetic is not supported on timestamp without time zone
now() is cast via the session TimeZone, shifting the cut-off
now() returns the time the server started, not the current time
Comparisons between timestamp types always return NULL in Postgres
questions.why: now() is timestamptz; comparing it with a plain timestamp casts it to local time in the session's TimeZone, so a session set to Europe/London in summer shifts the window by an hour. Using timestamptz columns, or a UTC session, avoids it. now() is the transaction start time.
questions.asked: Time zone bugs are subtle and costly, and knowing the implicit cast is expert-level.

questions.q: A sync job fetches `WHERE id > @lastSeenId ORDER BY id` every minute to pick up new rows. Why can it miss rows in Postgres or SQL Server?
choices: Identity values are reused after a delete, so old ids reappear
ORDER BY id is not guaranteed to be ascending without an index
Ids are assigned at insert, so a lower id can commit later
The job's READ COMMITTED snapshot hides every row inserted since it began
questions.why: Transaction A takes id 101 and commits slowly; B takes 102 and commits first. The job reads 102, stores it as the cursor, and never sees 101. Using an overlap window, a commit-ordered change feed (CDC, logical replication) or an outbox avoids it. Identities are not reused.
questions.asked: Incremental sync by id or timestamp is common, and this race causes silent data loss.

questions.q: In Postgres, what does adding a foreign key as `NOT VALID` and later running `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` achieve on a large live table?
choices: It skips checking existing rows forever while still checking new ones
It creates the constraint on a replica first and then copies it back
It lets you add the constraint without creating an index on the column
The add is quick; validation scans under a lighter lock
questions.why: `ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID` enforces the rule for new writes immediately without scanning existing rows; `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` then scans with a lock that allows normal reads and writes. Adding it in one step blocks writes during the full check. The same trick works for CHECK constraints.
questions.asked: Knowing how to add constraints without an outage is a hallmark of production Postgres experience.

questions.q: The intent is 'toys or games costing over 10'. Rows are (a, 5, toys), (b, 20, toys), (c, 5, games), (d, 20, games). Which names come back?
choices: b, c and d
b and d, as intended
d only
a, b, c and d
questions.why: AND binds tighter than OR, so this reads as `(price > 10 AND toys) OR games`, and cheap game c slips through. Parenthesise the OR: `price > 10 AND (category = 'toys' OR category = 'games')`, or use `category IN ('toys', 'games')`.
questions.asked: Operator precedence bugs in WHERE clauses return plausible-looking wrong data, so reviewers look for missing parentheses.

questions.q: A list endpoint uses `ORDER BY id LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20`. Which rows does it return?
choices: Rows 20 to 29 of the ordered result
Rows 21 to 30 of the ordered result
Rows 11 to 20 of the ordered result
Rows 1 to 10, starting after id 20
questions.why: OFFSET skips that many rows and LIMIT then takes the next ten, so page 3 of ten-per-page is rows 21 to 30 (`OFFSET (page - 1) * size`). OFFSET counts rows, not id values, which only coincide when ids have no gaps.
questions.asked: Off-by-one page maths is a common API bug, and knowing OFFSET counts rows sets up the keyset discussion.
